22500: Anuran larvae are dependent on water for survival and must adapt to xeric conditions in order to inhabit desert communities and survive. Many of these larval adaptations for individual species of desert anurans have been documented. However, little is known about the population biology and community interaction. A few studies have investigated competition related to predation and the age-structure of the anuran desert community, but temporal succession and spatial partitioning have been overlooked. Adaptations such as temporal succession and spatial partitioning could compensate for a shorter breeding period and smaller breeding area associated with a xeric habitat. Anuran succession has been discovered in other ecological communities and could explain the survival of anuran community inhabiting the Sonoran/Chihuahuan desert grassland. We investigated patterns of temporal and spatial structure of this anuran desert community to develop hypotheses regarding the mechanisms of the assemblages and gain insight into conserving and protecting these fragile communities.

22501: The African pygmy sleepers, genus Kribia, are eleotrid fishes endemic to the Nile River and West African freshwaters. Eight taxa, including four subspecies, have been assigned to this genus which was described by Herre in 1946. Taxa are currently delimited primarily by small differences in meristic characters. Morphological and meristic character variation was explored using principal components analysis. Graphic depiction of principal components scores displayed some evidence of clustering by both character types, but there was no clearly interpretable taxonomic or geographic pattern of distinction. Variation of cephalic neuromast patterns and pigmentation features has also been uninformative. Extensive collections of new specimens and tissue samples from the Fouta Djalon and upper Niger basin in Guinea may allow some clarification for that region.

22502: Nearly two decades ago one of the most influential publications for North American freshwater fishes evolved as a collaborative project edited by C. H. Hocutt and E. O. Wiley, The Zoogeography of North American Freshwater Fishes. It originated as a special symposium with ASIH and was successful for many reasons, one being strong interactions among participants before, at, and after the symposium. Contributions to the zoogeography book targeted specific regions of North America and provided tabular reviews of not only diversity of species known from different drainages and their status but also reviewed the geologies/hydrologies of areas as pertaining to fishes, biogeographies (faunal similarities or phylogenetics), and fossil histories. Without doubt, this book quickly galvanized many academic disciplines, in addition to systematic and taxonomic ichthyology, to conduct research on North American fishes. As a result, the last twenty years have been extremely productive in North America with respect to inventories, conservation of fishes, phylogeny generation across taxonomic ranks, community ecology and evolution, and comparative biogeography. We are revisiting this concept but at a New World scale - uniting expertise from North, Central, and South America for the development of new volumes entitled The Zoogeography of New World Freshwater Fishes. This will be a community- based effort like the model for the zoogeography book; we invite participants willing to work together at an international scale but focusing on particular geographic areas and drainage systems to provide faunistic, geological, systematic, and biogeographical information for chapters of this initiative. We are in the planning stages of this initiative and invite participants and ideas on content and identification of chapters for Central and South America. This is an important initiative and is consistent with NSF initiatives in BS&I, REVSYS, PBI, and AToL.

22503: The Grotto Salamander, Typhlotriton spelaeus is a troglobitic species that resides in Ozark Plateau caves from southwestern Missouri to extreme northeastern Kansas and adjacent areas of northern Arkansas and northeastern Oklahoma. Larval T. spelaeus inhabit mountain brooks, springs, and cave entrances, whereas the blind adult is typically found in the twilight and dark zones of wet caves, underground streams, and sinkholes. Little is known about the helminth parasites of this enigmatic salamander. Thirty-eight larval and adult T. spelaeus, were borrowed from the Arkansas State University Museum Herpetological (ASUMZ) collection and examined for helminth parasites. These salamanders had been collected from various locales in Independence, Izard, Sharp, and Stone counties, Arkansas, and Boone, Howell, and Taney counties, Missouri. In addition, eight larval T. spelaeus were collected in March 2003 from two caves in Shannon County, Missouri. Seven (18%) of the ASUMZ salamanders harbored infections, including one (2.6%) with the trematode, Plagioporus gyrinophili, two (5.3%) with the cestode, Bothriocephalus typhlotritonis, five (13.2%) with the nematode, Amphibiocapillaria tritonispunctati, and one (2.6%) with the acanthocephalan, Fessisentis vancleavei. In addition, all eight (100%) larval T. spelaeus from Shannon County, Missouri, harbored a neascus type metacercariae of a strigeoid trematode in their gills and body tissues. Plagioporus gyrinophili and F. vancleavei represent new helminth records for this host; new geographic distributional records are recorded for P. gyrinophili and B. typhlotritonis.

22504: To examine movement patterns and home range size, eastern hognose snakes (Heterodon platirhinos) were collected and surgically implanted with radio transmitters. After release, snakes were located approximately every 48 h, and the radiolocations were recorded using a hand-held GPS unit. Straight-line distances between locations were measured to approximate the distance moved between successive locations as well as the total distance moved throughout the active season. Minimum convex polygon (MCP) and fixed kernel (FK) home ranges were calculated for each snake. Additionally, to examine use of the home range, we tested for spatial randomness of the radiolocations within the 100% MCP home range. Snakes moved an average of 60.5 m per day and showed a range of total movements per active season from 903.4-6952.7 m. 100% MCP home ranges varied from 2.5-53.5 ha (mean=14.0 ha) and 95% FK home ranges varied from 2.2- 76.1 ha (mean=17.6 ha). Eight of nine snakes exhibited a non-random usage pattern within their 100% MCP home range. Spatial and temporal comparisons among individuals and among reproductive classes will be reported.

22505: I present phylogenetic analyses of crotaphytid lizards (Crotaphytus and Gambelia) based on morphological and molecular data. The previously published morphological data provided a biogeographically sensible, yet relatively weakly supported phylogenetic estimate for the group. Analysis of 1700 bp of mitochondrial DNA sequence data (1200 bp drawn from the protein- coding ND2 gene and flanking tRNA sequences and 600 bp representing the cytochrome b protein-coding gene) for all 12 recognized crotaphytid species (approximately 80 individuals sequenced) provides a well-supported and substantially incongruent estimate of crotaphytid phylogeny. Here I present analyses of the individual data sets as well as combined-data analyses undertaken within a Bayesian framework and attempt to explain the discrepancy and implications for crotaphytid biogeography. In a number of instances, the mtDNA data are inconsistent with monophyly of crotaphytid species. In at least two cases, inferred polyphyly of species can be clearly attributed to recent or past hybridization between non-sister species with consequent mitochondrial introgression.

22506: Large-scale ecological analyses of marine systems are limited by the availability of uniform, high-resolution environmental data. Worldwide data sets from satellites are now available, providing moderate-to-high spatial, temporal and spectral resolutions. Extensive use has been made of these data in commercial fisheries research. Nevertheless, the utility of these data sets in answering questions about large-scale biotic patterns has gone largely unexplored. If useful, remotely sensed data would represent a massive increase in the amount of environmental data available to marine researchers. In this contribution, the utility of remotely sensed data in predictive ecological niche modeling analyses is investigated. These initial proof-of-concept analyses will address whether satellite data can be used as ecological/environmental data in modeling niches and predicting distributions of individual fish species in the Gulf of Mexico. Data from the Moderate resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) sensor is used, along with individual species occurrence data, in predictive ecological niche modeling analyses using the Genetic Algorithm for Rule-set Prediction (GARP).

22507: Variation in carapace morphology has significant implications for the success of juvenile turtles, though this topic has received little analytical attention. Specifically, the three-dimensional shape of the carapace affects performance in all turtles, including hydrodynamic streamlining (particularly important to highly aquatic species), structural integrity, and other properties. In order to test performance-related hypotheses, three-dimensional variation in carapace morphology was quantified in a clutch of Podocnemis unifilis, the Yellow-Spotted Amazon River turtle. The examination of clutchmates permits the lowest possible morphological variation due to genetic differences among specimens, though multiple paternity within the clutch is a possibility. Nonetheless, we identify regions of significant morphological variation in vertebral and costal scutes, arguably the most structurally important portions of the turtle carapace. Individuals exhibiting variations in localized morphology are easily identified and cluster into a few morphotypes. In addition to this cross-sectional analysis of shape in a clutch, we present preliminary data on growth within the clutch. Both positively and negatively allometric growth of the vertebral scutes is evident after only the first few months post-hatching, indicating significant shape change in this time of high mortality. This report on initial variation in morphology marks the start of a longitudinal study of the effects of diet on growth rate and morphology in P. unifilis.

22508: Two subspecies of the dipsadine snake Imantodes gemmistratus are currently considered to occur in western Mexico: I. g. latistratus and I. g. gracillimus. Once considered to represent distinct species, these taxa were relegated to subspecies status based on putative intermediate specimens from northern Jalisco. During recent herpetological surveys of western Mexico, we collected specimens of both subspecies from southern Nayarit that appeared to exhibit distinctive phenotypes despite occurring in apparent sympatry. The collection of this material prompted us to examine the relationships of these samples using mitochondrial DNA sequence data. Herein we report the preliminary results from phylogenetic analyses including samples of all species and subspecies of Imantodes occurring in Mexico.

22509: Land use, such as timber harvesting, degrades much of the remaining habitat available to wildlife. Information on practices that can mitigate the impacts of land use is needed. In 1993 and 1994, we used monthly samples (April through September) of water conditions and amphibian captures in dip nets and funnel traps to evaluate amphibian use of 22 manmade pools on haul roads in clear- cut units of a timber sale on McGowan Mountain, Tucker County, West Virginia. Pools ranged in size from 4.6 to 27.9 m2 (mean 9.9 m2) and from 7.7 to 37.0 cm in depth (mean 20.6 cm). The clear-cut units were closed 1-6 months before the pools were constructed. Eleven ponds in 1993 and 15 of 22 pools in 1994 were used as breeding sites for amphibians. Anurans that used the ponds included Bufo a. americanus, Rana sylvatica, Pseudacris brachyphona, and Hyla chrysoscelis. Other amphibians that occupied the ponds but were not found to use them to breed included Rana clamitans melanota and two species of urodelans, Desmognathus ochrophaeus, and Gyrinophilus p. porphyriticus. Amphibians did not breed in pools that dried early in the summer before larval development was complete in other ponds; and concentrations of both magnesium and sodium were significantly higher in ponds used by breeding amphibians. This research suggests that the building of vernal pools in clear-cut areas provides usable breeding habitat for anurans and refugia for some salamander species; however, hydrology and water chemistry may affect whether amphibians will use artificial ponds.

22510: We describe several aspects of the ecology of Aparasphenodon brunoi, a species highly associated with bromeliads. We comment on the relationships of this species with bromeliad size, pattern of microhabitat use, reproduction, sexual dimorphism, and diet. This study was conducted on a Restinga habitat near Presidente Kennedy, Espirito Santo, southeastern coast of Brazil. When the animals were found inside the bromeliads, we measure bromeliad and head size of frogs. We analyzed stomach contents and determined the sex and reproductive condition. We found 17 individuals (58.62%) in bromeliad leafs, six (20.69%) in Cactaceae, three (10.34%) in liana and three (10.34%) on trunks. The correlation between head measurements and bromeliad size were high, indicating that animals choose bromeliads based on their size, to minimize water loss. The most common prey items were beetles, ants, and insect larvae, suggesting that the species is a generalist. The smallest reproductive female and male had 34.47 mm and 46.53 mm of SVL, respectively. Aparasphenodon brunoi showed significant sexual dimorphism with females having larger bodies than males.

22511: Leptodeira annulata have the widest geographical range in the genus, from Mexico to southeastern Brazil, being currently divided into 5 subspecies. In Venezuela two subspecies have been reported: L. annulata annulata, L. a . ashmeadi (as weel as L. bakeri and L. septentrionalis ornata). Leptodeira a. ashmeadi has a geographic distribution spanning part of the northern of the country, except the highest portions of the Andean mountains exhibiting a high variability in body proportions, scale number and colouration pattern; 182 specimens of L. a. ashmeadi, and 19 of L. bakeri were examined for external morphology characters; tissue and blood samples were taken from 21 specimens of Venezuelan L. a. ashmeadi, 1 L. a. annulata (from Surinam), 2 L. septentrionalis (1 from Belize, 1 from Ecuador), and 1 Imantodes cenchoa (from Venezuela, outgroup). A multivariate morphometric and a sequence of 401 bp of the cytochrome b gene using the PCR technique, and phylogeny evaluated mainly Maximum Parsimony, and Maximum Likelihood algorithms, trying to determine whether more than one lineage occur within L. a. ashmeadi. Multivariate analysis confirm the distinction of L. bakeri as a different species and most of the specimens of L. a ashmeadi were plotted together, but populations from northwestern and western Venezuela were partially segregated from L. a. ashmeadi main group. The phylogenetic analysis suggest the monophyly of the genus Leptodeira but fail to define a intrageneric hypothesis of relationships due to low support values for most of the nodes in the three phylogenetic analysis. Additional morphological characters from more specimens, and tissue samples of L. a. ashmeadi, as well as from the other species present in Venezuela and adjacent countries would be necessary for a more accurate resolution of the systematic of the genus Leptodeira in Venezuela.

22512: The Black Croaker, Cheilotrema saturnum (Girard), is a common member of the nearshore fish assemblage off Southern California. Overnight gill nets were set bimonthly from April to October from 1995 to 2003 to sample the nearshore ichthyofauna. Specimens ranged from 126 to 362mm standard length and 40 to 750g total weight. The mainland was found to support a significantly greater population than the offshore Channel Islands. Conversely, specimens captured at the Channel Island were significantly than those from the mainland. The sex ratios over age and length indicated a gonochoric pattern, with the primary spawning period being late spring early summer based on gonosomatic indices. Catch per unit effort (CPUE) data suggests the Palos Verdes Peninsula supported the largest population sampled within the Southern California Bight.

22513: This is the third year of our study of the reproductive ecology of the Small-mouthed Salamander, Ambystoma texanum. We completely enclosed a small (250 m2), ephemeral, man-made pond on the campus of Missouri Valley College with a drift fence and pit-fall traps in early February of 2002 and continued to monitor the fence daily throughout the breeding seasons. In our presentation we will compare the 2002, 2003, and 2004 field seasons; however, at the time of abstract submission we only have data for 2002 and 2003. We collected the first salamanders on 20 February 2002 and 12 March 2003, which was prior to the pond filling with water on 20 April 2002 and 17 April 2003. In 2002, 67% of the individuals entered the pond from the north, but only 42% entered from the north in 2003. Residential areas, the MVC campus, and a small wooded area are to the north of the pond. Sex ratio was highly male-biased in both years (1.8:1; 3.0:1), with male numbers remaining nearly identical (N = 86 & 88) and females decreasing between the two years (N = 47 & 29). In 2002 salamander larvae were relatively abundant, but we documented only 5 juveniles leaving the pond before the pond dried on 3 July. In 2003 salamanders laid eggs, but we did not observe larvae and no juveniles emerged before the pond dried on 27 June. The spring and summer of both 2002 and 2003 were extremely dry; the pond filled late (well after the normal breeding season) and dried early. However, this year the pond filled with water on 10 December 2003 and currently (Jan. 2004) holds water. We predict that this will benefit recruitment by allowing breeding to occur much earlier (as much 4-6 weeks) than in the previous two years.

22514: The Texas horned lizard (Phrynosoma cornutum) has experienced apparent large-scale declines throughout its range, particularly in Texas. We studied the effect of prescribed burning (a habitat management practice of increasing popularity) on the ecology of the Texas horned lizard in a thornscrub savanna. We assessed home range size, habitat selection, survival rates, and prey abundance of horned lizards in 4 treatments. Home ranges in the summer-burned-grazed treatment were smaller than those in the other treatments (winter-burned-grazed, unburned- grazed, and unburned-ungrazed). Survival rates in burned sites were higher than in unburned. The survival functions also differed between burning treatments, with survival declining in early summer in the unburned areas and in late summer in the burned areas. Lizards selected for Whitebrush (Aloysia gratissima) and avoided Texas Persimmon (Diospyros texana) consistently across treatments. Selection or avoidance of other woody species was not consistent among treatments. Smaller home ranges in the summer-burned treatment suggest that lizards are finding prey and cover in a smaller area, indicating a beneficial effect of summer burning. Ant activity, used as a surrogate of ant abundance, has been historically higher on burned sites on our study area. Therefore, more food, or better food-cover interspersion, may explain the higher survival in burned areas and the smaller home ranges in summer-burned areas. We conclude that prescribed burning in a thornscrub savanna provided favorable ecological conditions for Texas horned lizards.

22515: We examined evaporative water loss (EWL) rates in two species of pitvipers to determine if a shift to aquatic habitats has allowed for increased EWL rate in Agkistrodon piscivorus (an aquatic species), relative to a species representing the putatively ancestral condition (A. contortrix, a terrestrial species). Additionally, we examined intraspecific variation in EWL rate for both species as a response to two 10-day humidity acclimation treatments. In the first part of the study, A. piscivorus was found to have higher EWL rates than A. contortrix, and snakes in wet acclimation treatments had higher rates than those in dry treatments, as predicted. Individuals of A. piscivorus exhibited EWL rates of 150 and 87 mg h-1 (wet and dry acclimation, respectively), while individuals of A. contortrix had rates of 102 and 87 mg h-1. In the second part of the study, individuals were reacclimated to the opposite acclimation treatment as in the first part. The order in which individuals were placed in their respective acclimation treatments (wet-dry vs. dry-wet) affected EWL rates. Individuals experiencing the wet-dry acclimation order exhibited reduced plasticity in acclimation-induced EWL rate responses as compared to those that underwent the dry acclimation first. The low EWL rates found in Agkistrodon, in conjunction with previous studies on EWL in other snakes, suggest that phylogenetic conservatism with respect to EWL rate may exist in the family Viperidae. Nonetheless, EWL rate may vary among viperid species via small adaptive changes, such as those observed in the current study.

22516: The Mullidae include six genera and about 55 species. In this study, a hypothesis for the phylogenetic relationship of these genera based on an analysis of osteological characters is proposed. Besides having a pair of chin barbels, monophyly of this family is supported by some additional apomorphic characters including presences of (1) a small round cartilage between the dorsal hypohyals, (2) additional scapular foramens, (3) a socket formed on the interopercle to receive the epihyal. Topology of the hypothetical phylogenetic tree is the following: (Parupeneus, Pseudupeneus), (Upeneichthys, (Upeneus, (Mullus, Mulloidichthys))). Syapomorphic characters supporting this hypothesis include: presence of only two predorsal bones, absence of uroneural 2, second dorsal spine not interlocked with the first dorsal pterygiophore, relative position of the posterior corner the palatine and the front border of the orbital cavity, presence of prezygopophyses on the abdominal vertebrae, and morphology of the dorsal hypohyal. Autapomorphic characters of Mullus and Parupeneus are related to the shape of the basihyal and distance between the two chin pores, respectively.

22517: Foraging modes generally fall along a continuous spectrum between ambush foraging (sit-and- wait) and active foraging (widely foraging). Foraging mode affects, and is affected by, ecological, behavioral, thermal, reproductive and bioenergetic constraints. To examine energy allocation decisions associated with foraging mode we compared two syntopic crotaline snakes that differ in foraging mode. The copperhead (Agkistrodon contortrix) is an active forager, while the timber rattlesnake (Crotalus horridus) is an ambush forager. We conducted a mark recapture study from 1995-2003 and radiotracked male copperheads and timber rattlesnakes between 2001 and 2003. At time of capture we collected data on sex, SVL, reproductive and foraging behavior. During radiotracking we collected location, body temperature, behavior, and habitat characteristics. We used fecal analysis and stable isotope analysis to determine diet of each species. Gravid females were retained in the lab until parturition to estimate reproductive effort. We measured field metabolic rate, standard metabolic rate, and specific dynamic action. Copperheads at our site have a more streamlined body form, smaller home range, greater movement rate, more diverse diet, and a lower reproductive effort than timber rattlesnakes, suggesting that the copperhead is an active forager. We compared energy allocated to competing compartments (maintenance, activity, and SDA) and drew inferences about the surplus energy available to each species for growth and reproduction.

22518: The rattle of rattlesnakes is part of a complex system that also includes many anatomical and physiological specializations relative to the tails of other snakes. The sustained, fast movements of rattling suggest that rattling evolved from the fast movements of defensive tail vibration rather than from caudal luring or another behavior involving slow movements. However, the evolution of tail vibration in snakes has not been well studied. Based on literature records of defensive tail vibration, we mapped this behavior onto a phylogeny of snakes and tested whether tail vibration was an ancestral behavior in rattlesnakes, pitvipers, and colubroids. Tail vibration occurs in Xenopeltis, at least one boid, 30 or more colubrids, 3 elapids, and 11 non-rattlesnake viperids; therefore, it evolved in basal snakes, was apparently lost in some lineages, and was ancestral in pitvipers. To study the evolution of tail vibration and rattling performance, we also measured the tail vibration frequencies in several species of rattlesnakes, copperheads and cottonmouths, and several species of colubrids. Tail vibration frequencies are moderately high in colubrids, appear to be slightly higher in copperheads and cottonmouths, and are highest in rattlesnakes. These phylogenetic and physiological results suggest that tail vibration was probably the behavioral precursor to rattling, and that the high levels of tail vibration performance evolved gradually before the rattle itself evolved.

22519: In an era of emerging infectious diseases, understanding the associated ecological consequences is a significant challenge. Threatened herpetofauna populations already at risk from human development can be further impacted by disease. Upper Respiratory Tract Disease (URTD) has recently emerged in wild populations of the gopher tortoise (Gopherus polyphemus), and with it come major conservation implications. Supporting over 360 animal species in its burrows, the tortoise is an ecologically critical component of xeric upland habitats in the southeastern United States. Throughout much of the species’ range, populations are reduced to small fractions of their former sizes because of human development on upland habitats and the emergence of URTD could further impact many of these populations. While much attention has been paid to increasing our understanding of clinical aspects of URTD, very little is known about the ecology of the disease. Anthropogenic disturbances such as tortoise relocations and habitat alteration coincide with the emergence of the disease - making it unclear if URTD occurs naturally but has been exacerbated by human encroachment, or if the disease has materialized only recently. Thus, a multidisciplinary research project funded by the National Science Foundation is investigating the impact of the disease on wild tortoise population dynamics and health, and specifically on the influence of anthropogenic disturbance on disease transmission. Preliminary results from serological and molecular diagnostic tests confirm the widespread prevalence of the disease throughout tortoise populations in central and northern Florida. We will present GIS images tracing the concurrence of urban development with the incidence of disease.

22520: Sand-diving, a quick and forceful headfirst plunge into the substrate to completely cover the body, has been documented in three fish families: Creediidae, Trichonotidae and Labridae. Behavioral observations show that this is a predator avoidance behavior; however the kinematics of sand-diving remain unstudied. We used high-speed video to describe and analyze sand-diving by the Slippery Dick Wrasse, Halichoeres bivittatus (Labridae). Eight captive H. bivittatus individuals were persuaded to bury in two substrate types: fine sand or coarsely crushed coral. The event duration of the sand-diving behavior ranged from 1.7- 3.6 seconds. The frequencies of lateral body undulation varied from 2 to 18 Hz, decreasing with time since initiation of behavior. Undulatory amplitudes were inversely proportional to frequency, with amplitude values ranging from 1 cm at high undulatory frequency, to greater than 7 cm at low frequency. Quantitative analysis shows that sand-diving and subsequent burying of H. bivittatus is distinguished by distinct phases of undulatory axial body movements. The first phase is characterized by high frequencies and low amplitude; the second is characterized by low frequencies and high amplitude of body undulations. The initial high frequency undulation may serve to create a slurry of substrate and water through which the animal is capable of swimming. To compensate for differences in substrate density, H. bivittatus varies undulatory frequency and amplitude. These behavioral modifications provide equivalent burying times despite differences in substrate types. A comparison of kinematics of other species of Labridae that exhibit sand-diving would provide an interesting comparison of movement based on body shape and ecology.

22521: Food habits and size composition of a snake community in Ampijoroa, a tropical dry forest in northwestern Madagascar, were studied. Field surveys were conducted from the end of the dry season to the middle of the rainy season in 1999 and from 2000 to 2001. A total of four months survey yielded captures of 259 individuals, which were comprised of eighteen species and three families (13 colubrids, two boids, and three typhlopids). Snout-vent length and body mass of these snakes ranged from 92 mm to 1840 mm and 0.5 g to 4520 g, respectively, showing a continuous diversity of size composition. The most abundant species is Mimophis mahfalensis (86 individuals), followed by Leioheterodon madagascariensis (44), Dromicodryas bernieri (24), and Madagascarophis colubrinus (25). We recovered 155 prey items from the stomach contents of 64 individuals, which consisted of 12 species. 22523: The eastern extension of the massive Trans-Mexican Neovolcanic Belt (TMNB) contacts the Atlantic Coast in central Veracruz, Mexico. 22525: The Flat-tailed Horned Lizard (Phrynosoma mcallii) has a restricted distribution in SE California, SW Arizona, and adjacent Mexico and has been the subject of extensive conservation efforts and expenditures. 22526: Male boreal toads are thought to return to the breeding site year after year and, if absent in a particular year, be even more likely to be present the following year. Using Pollock's Robust Design we estimated temporary emigration (the probability that a male toad is absent from breeding sites) at two locations in Rocky Mountain National Park. We present data that indicate that not only do male toads not return to the breeding site every year, but may be absent for multiple years. Estimates of both γ parameters (γ' = probability that a male toad is absent from the breeding site at time t+1 if absent at time t; γ" = probability that a male toad is absent at time t+ 1 if present at time t) were high, average γ> 0.5. Although we suspected that the probability of temporary emigration would be state dependent (Markovian, e.g. where a toad is at time t affects where he will be at time t+1), we were unable to differentiate between random and Markovian processes of temporary emigration. We also hypothesized relationships between temporary emigration and a number of environmental variables, but none of the models reflecting these hypotheses performed well in the model selection process.

22527: Proportion of area occupied (PAO) by a species is a widely used concept in ecology; from monitoring programs, to metapopulation studies, to species-habitat models (including resource selection probability functions). Within ARMI, PAO is used at various scales as a mid-level monitoring metric of population status (e.g., for monitoring amphibian populations within reserves, national parks or at a regional scale). Generally, the basic design for studies to estimate PAO involves conducting presence/absence surveys for the target species at a number of habitat patches or monitoring sites. However, it is widely accepted that the absence of a species can never be confirmed and often there may be a reasonable chance the species was actually present, but went undetected. As such, an estimate of PAO that does not account for the imperfect detectability of a species may be biased, and particularly there may be an observed change in PAO caused solely by a change in detectability rather than a real change in PAO. This has long been realized by field workers who have often used the protocol of conducting multiple presence/absence surveys in a relatively short period of time, with species absence being assumed if the species was never detected in any of the multiple surveys of the site. Although with data of this type, it is possible to go one better and use some simple modeling techniques to obtain unbiased estimates of PAO (and related parameters) and detection probabilities. Furthermore, information on habitat types, weather conditions, etc. can be directly incorporated into the modeling process. In this talk I will briefly review the concepts behind some recently developed modeling approaches (with minimal equations) and discuss some simple tips that should be kept in mind when designing a study to estimate PAO.

22528: Venoms are complex secretions which are produced in specialized glands of a large number of colubroid snakes, and a primary role is to incapacitate prey remotely and/or facilitate prey handling. Among rattlesnakes, venom composition often (but not always) varies ontogentically, and this variation also tracks changes in dominant prey type. Venom composition is genetically determined and therefore is directly related to phylogeny; however, within specific lineages, venom composition varies considerably. We have analyzed venoms of numerous rattlesnake species from the perspective of placing venom biochemistry into broader biological contexts. Extensive interactions between environmental constraints, diet, age and phylogenetic relations exist, but a hierarchical relationship is apparent. Within the constraints of relatedness of taxa, there is considerable flexibility in absolute venom composition which appears to be related primarily to diet and secondarily to environment. As an example of one noted trend, highly toxic venoms generally lack high concentrations of metalloproteases, enzymes responsible for much of the structural damage resulting from envenomation; conversely, those with potent metalloprotease activity generally lack neurotoxins. Though there are numerous other components which vary with the above factors, the interplay of toxicity versus tissue damaging effects follows a predictable trend. Extension of these generalizations to colubroid snake venom composition will also be discussed.

22529: Venoms of snakes of the polyphyletic family Colubridae offer an immense opportunity for the discovery of novel biological compounds and new structural variants, and few colubrid species have been thoroughly studied. We initiated a study of Brown Treesnake (Boiga irregularis) venom composition with the general goal of identifying all dominant protein species. Yields of up to 25 mg per extraction have been obtained from large individuals. Venoms were analyzed using enzyme assays, one and two dimensional electrophoresis, HPLC, MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry and N-terminal sequencing. Numerous toxins are present in treesnake venoms, including metalloproteases, acetycholinesterases and helveprins. Based on N-terminal sequence, one of the smaller toxins (9.9 kD) is a homolog of several of the weak neurotoxins present in elapid venoms. Two-dimensional electrophoresis of neonate and adult snake venoms indicates a high degree of similarity of venoms from different age classes; however, metalloproteases are more abundant in the adult snake venoms, and there is an effect of ontogeny on venom composition as is observed in other venomous species. Brown treesnake venom contains many components found in other snake venoms, and as sequence data is accumulated, inferences about the evolution of these toxins will become possible. Although compounds unique to colubrid snakes are also present, it is clear that colubrid venoms are homologous with the venoms of front-fanged snakes.

22530: A central paradigm emerging from analysis of venom components is that venomous reptiles have usurped numerous regulatory components of vertebrate systems and redirected them against prey. By introducing these proteins into prey tissues at physiologically inappropriate times and concentrations, homeostasis is rapidly compromised. An example of this phenomenon is provided by the diversity of serine proteases in venoms. In addition to frequent occurrence of severe tissue damage, bites by many viperid snakes result in prolonged disturbance of hemostasis (coagulopathies). Several different serine proteases are common among viperid snake venoms, and these enzymes are the primary agents which interfere with hemostasis of vertebrates. Using a single step RP-HPLC method, a thrombin-like protease (tigrinobin) was isolated from venom of Crotalus tigris, a species with limited distribution in the Sonoran desert which produces a venom with high toxicity and low metalloprotease activity; MALDI-TOF-MS indicated a mass of 29.1 kD. Tigrinobin greatly accelerated prothrombin time of freshly collected citrated human plasma and promoted rapid clot formation in fibrinogen clotting assays. Tigrinobin shows 100% N- terminal sequence homology with venombin A from Lachesis muta and several other viperid venom thrombin-like proteases, but its sequence is quite different from bovine or human thrombin. Time course assays indicated that tigrinobin rapidly catalyzed the release of fibrinopeptide A, and a second peptide was more slowly released. Like other venom thrombin- like proteases, tigrinobin shows superficial similarities to mammalian thrombin but has significant differences from thrombin. Thrombin-like proteases are largely responsible for the rapid onset of fibrinogen depletion and subsequent inability to form clots commonly seen upon envenomation by many viperid snakes of prey or humans. Like other venom components, tigrinobin represents a homolog of normal regulatory enzymes which act to deregulate critical homeostatic processes.

22531: A continuing challenge in evolutionary ecology is to determine whether individual phenotypic differences within populations are adaptive polymorphisms or non-adaptive variation around an adaptive mean. Within-population relationships between trophic polymorphism and resource use offer good opportunities to examine adaptive individual variation within and among environments. In this study we used geometric morphometric methods to compare cranial morphology and diets of adult red-backed salamanders (Plethodon cinereus) from two habitat types (upland and lowland forest) at five sites in upstate New York. We found that variation in salamander trophic morphology related to changes in diet between habitats, within populations, and within habitats. Across populations, salamander morphology showed a consistent change between lowland and upland habitats that was correlated with prey use. Within habitats we found the same relationship between head shape and diet observed between habitats. Among the key prey associated with habitat-typical morphologies were several nonnative species. Our results are consistent with previous Plethodon studies on food use as an ecological constraint. We hypothesize that changes in the invertebrate community, consistent with differences in habitat, is driving micro-geographic variation in salamander cranial morphology. In particular, these changes may be driven by the invasive of nonnative prey which differ in their distribution between upland and lowland forests. This raises the possibility that introduced species are having an unintended evolutionary effect on salamander populations.

22533: Temperature has a dramatic influence on a wide array of physiological functions (e.g., development, growth, locomotion, digestion, immune response). As a result, it is essential for most organisms to regulate their body temperature to at least some extent. Since ectotherms, including reptiles, cannot produce their own heat as do mammals and birds, they must selectively utilize various microhabitats within their environment to effectively thermoregulate. The constraints of an environment can dramatically affect the behaviorof an ectotherm, its physiology, and even its geographic distribution. Thermal responses in western diamond-backed rattlesnakes (Crotalus atrox) were studied using semi-continuous (bi-hourly) thermal profiles from both the environment and individual snakes using radiotelemetry and miniature temperature data loggers collected over a period of two years. Thermal profiles have been compared between the sexes and through varied physiologic states (e.g., reproductively active, reproductively inactive, post- prandially, and during the over-wintering period) to elucidate relationships between snakes and their environment. Results suggest that snakes are closely tied to thermal constraints within their environment, inducing daily and seasonal shifts in behavior and microhabitat selection.

22536: We investigated the distribution, population biology, and habitat preferences of dwarf seahorses (Hippocampus zosterae) and their pipefish relatives (syngnathid fishes) in the Florida Keys, USA. 22537: Studies on female reproductive biology of the Brown Treesnake (Boiga irregularis), an invasive predator on Guam, indicate that reproduction is not seasonal and may even be acyclic. Females with enlarged ovarian follicles or oviductal eggs occur in all months of the year. Proximate factors that elicit initiation of ovarian growth in individuals are therefore not readily apparent and it is unknown whether they are primarily exogenous or endogenous. When maintained in captivity under constant environmental conditions (≈24ºC) and fed ad libitum, females do not become reproductive. However, when exposed to a period of cool temperatures (≈60 days at ≈20ºC) females initiate ovarian growth in synchrony, thus implicating temperature fluctuation as an important proximate cue. Temperatures on Guam, however, show little monthly variation, and if females were responding to even small temperature changes, then they should do so in synchrony (but apparently do not). Thus, if temperature is the proximate cue on Guam, it is enigmatic how females experience temperatures cool enough to induce ovarian growth. We hypothesize that reproduction on Guam requires individual females to periodically seek out and reside in microclimates cool enough to initiate a reproductive cycle. Factors influencing female reproduction in other Boiga species are contrasted.

22538: The reproductive biology of male brown treesnakes (Boiga irregularis) on Guam was investigated to gain insight into whether this invasive species has traits (e.g., seasonality) that could be exploited using reproductive inhibition technology. Males reached sexual maturity at a relatively small body size (870-970 mm, snout-vent length), with the average male maturing at about 905 mm. All individuals were mature by about 1000 mm. Upon reaching maturity, males apparently remain constantly reproductive. All males in all months of the year had testes that were undergoing spermatogenesis, sperm in the epididymis and vas deferens, and cells in the kidney sexual segments (KSS) that were hypertrophied and secretory. The only features that varied significantly among months were plasma testosterone concentration, and KSS tubule diameter and epithelial height. Changes expected in other features if reproduction had some degree of seasonality (e.g., testes mass, seminiferous tubule epithelial height) were not observed. Although the apparent absence of reproductive seasonality may somewhat lessen the feasibility of using a male reproductive inhibitor as a control method, the constant availability of reproductive males makes it relatively simple to conduct evaluations of a diversity of potential inhibitors fairly rapidly.

22542: We surveyed fishes and environmental characteristics in 119 streams in the West Virginia highlands to identify natural and anthropogenic factors structuring fish assemblages. 22544: The Amazon Molly (a species of small, live bearing fish) is gynogenetic; the population consists only of females that mate with Sailfin Molly males. 22545: The extent to which communities in similar environments but different geographic regions exhibit convergence has long been debated. Using phylogenetic analyses based on mitochondrial DNA sequence data, we found that evolutionary convergence of ecological morphology occurs both in terms of pairs of ecomorphologically highly similar transcontinental pairs of species and of overall community-wide patterns. This result implies that deterministic adaptive evolution shapes community patterns and overrides the historical contingencies unique to particular lineages.

22549: Rattlesnake rattling involves sustaining high-frequency muscle contractions and high metabolic rates that exceed the maximum rates reported for most other vertebrate muscles. 22551: Shape variation is widespread in nature and embodies both a response to and a source for evolution and natural selection. Multivariate analysis of variance indicated that nesting area has a limited role in describing plastron shape variation among clutches, while differences between individual clutches were highly significant, suggesting a prominent clutch effect. The covariation between plastron shape and several possible maternal effect variables (yolk hormone levels and egg dimensions) was assessed, and found to be negligible. We subsequently employed two recently proposed methods for estimating heritability from these shape variables, and generalized the univariate approach to accommodate unequal sample sizes. Both the univariate and multivariate methods of estimating shape heritability yielded nearly equivalent values for both nesting populations (h2 ≈ 0.6 in all cases). However, we estimated the dominant trend in shape heritability for each nesting population and found that these directions were significantly different. Therefore, although the univariate approach is able to estimate the magnitude of shape heritability it is unable to accurately describe how shape has evolved. The results of this integration of evolutionary quantitative genetics and geometric morphometrics suggest that systematic studies on morphological characters undergoing similar concealed convergent evolution could yield misleading hypotheses of evolutionary relationships among taxa.

22553: Yellowfin Goby, an estuarine fish native to Japan, Korea, and China, was reported in the 1960s to have invaded San Francisco Bay (SFB) via commercial shipping, and to have then dramatically increased in population size. 22555: Temperature-dependent sex determination (TSD), the effect of embryonic incubation temperature on sex of hatchlings, occurs in all four extant orders of reptiles. All three populations exhibit Type 1b TSD (FM), where eggs incubated at 22ºC result in male hatchlings, while those incubated at 21ºC or lower produce predominantly female hatchlings. Key features are that, compared to other reptiles, tuatara eggs incubate successfully at low temperatures, sex is determined over a narrow transitional range of temperatures (TRT: as low as 1 C in some populations), and males are produced at warm temperatures. So far, little geographic variation is evident among populations. Populations of ectothermic animals restricted to islands are particularly vulnerable to effects of global warming. The sex ratio of tuatara on North Brother Island is significantly biased toward males (60%), and sex ratios at hatching on Stephens Island are similarly male-biased. Our studies are continuing to investigate the capacity of tuatara to adapt to rapid global warming, particularly the extent to which population persistence associated with unbalanced sex ratios may be threatened by rising ambient temperatures.

22559: We tested for differences in growth rate of Wood Frog (Rana sylvatica) tadpoles raised from egg masses obtained from four vernal ponds. 22560: The search for useful model systems in the study of sensory processing in vertebrate nervous systems has resulted in many neuroethological studies investigating the roles played by a single sensory modality in a given behavior. 22561: In 1974 Ernest Williams proposed that retrograde evolution could explain the unique toe morphology of two South American Anolis lizards. 22563: Lake Pontchartrain, an oligohaline estuary in southeastern Louisiana, has been subject to numerous anthropogenic impacts over the last half century including urban and agricultural runoff, shell dredging, over-fishing, artificial saltwater and freshwater inputs, shoreline alteration, and industrial discharges. 22564: Reports of postpartum parental care in squamate reptiles (lizards and snakes) are rare and generally anecdotal. 22565: Studies that have investigated why sequential hermaphroditism evolves in fishes have often included the size advantage model. 22567: The liparid Allocareproctus jordani (Burke) was collected in the Aleutian Islands during surveys conducted by the Alaska Fisheries Science Center, representing the first documented records for North America. 22568: Phylogenies and Classifications, fundamental information retrieval systems critical to a vast array of disciplines, provide efficient systems for organizing information, predictions and interpretations of descent of traits, lineages, and associations, and many meta-level biotic and abiotic patterns and processes. 22570: The wide regulation of metabolic and digestive performance to feeding and fasting experienced by Burmese pythons (Python molurus) is considered a physiological adaptation to their infrequent feeding. 22572: Male frogs use advertisement calls to attract mates and aggressive calls to ward off rivals. 22575: Much of the species-level diversity currently recognized by taxonomists is the result of phenotypic modifications that serve to enhance intra- or intersexual communication. 22577: Previous research has shown that rattlesnakes are capable of utilizing substrate odors to relocate envenomated prey when presented with competing odors and complex choice tests. 22579: Habitat choice and density-dependent dispersal must be considered when evaluating the effects of habitat change on animals. 22582: Some animals survive periods of adversely dry and/or hot climatic conditions through terrestrial dormancy, termed estivation. 22585: Conservation planners often act without adequate information on the life history patterns of declining species, especially those with extremely long lives because the data may take decades to collect. 22590: Existing theoretical and empirical work has shown that individual condition may influence the extent to which foragers choose to forage in productive, but risky habitats. Individuals in poor condition are predicted to take greater risks in productive habitats to obtain resources. 22593: Viviparity in reptiles is hypothesized to evolve in cold climates at high latitudes and high elevations through selection for progressively longer periods of egg retention. 22598: In spite of swimming the oceans for 450 million years, little is known of the cartilaginous skeleton of elasmobranchs. Here we compared the material and biochemical properties of both vertebral and jaw cartilages in sharks, skates, and rays. Collagen concentrations in the jaw are similar to those in the vertebrae. Proteoglycan in the vertebrae is generally two times that found in the jaw cartilage. Maximum strength is the same in both jaw and vertebral cartilage, although there are differences between species. Many of these differences may be due to mineralization found in vertebral cartilage. Just over half the dry weight of vertebrae can be mineral while the jaw cartilage has very little mineralization. The arrangement of the vertebral mineralization is also an important contributor to the differences in structural properties.

Molecular evidence suggests that carnivorous cheiline wrasses and herbivorous parrotfishes are closely related, providing an ideal group for comparing the evolution of functional systems. We used high-speed digital video to record feeding events of two carnivorous wrasses, Cheilinus fasciatus and Epibulus insidiator and two herbivorous parrotfishes, Scarus vetula and Sparisoma radians. Digitized morphological landmarks from feeding events provided data on: time and distance to prey, velocity, acceleration, body angle during approach, oral jaw movement, cranial elevation, fin movement, and oculomotor movement. The results show that carnivores and herbivores utilize different angles of approach during the feeding sequence, and that the timing of carnivore oral jaw movement is closely timed with fin stroke cycle, a pattern not seen in herbivores. Although eye movement patterns in both groups correlate with a decrease in velocity as a fish approaches a food item, carnivores' eyes were positioned forward during the feeding strike and move to center at or after the strike, whereas herbivores' eyes move laterally to center before the bite. Cheiline wrasses and parrotfishes exhibit consistent patterns of jaw, fin, and eye components during feeding; coordination differences between these fishes may represent adaptations to different trophic ecologies. Biomechanics and neuromuscular activity during coordination of feeding may clarify the role of sensory systems in this complex behavior and reveal patterns of evolution of divergent trophic strategies in coral reef fishes.

22611: Evolutionary divergence among anuran advertisement calls can act as a pre-mating isolation mechanism between incipient species. 22612: Anthropogenic habitat reduction and fragmentation are major causes of amphibian population declines and extinction. 22614: Semi-aquatic turtles of the family Emydidae typically thermoregulate by aerial basking. Basking behavior was studied in yearling Trachemys scripta to elicit information on the social aspects of this behavior. Choice experiments were conducted in an aquarium with a basking platform and lamp placed at each end. Turtles had a choice of basking alone or with a tethered, novel conspecific of equivalent size. During the three- hour test period, the typical pattern of events included a brief period of inactivity followed by a longer surveying phase, during which turtles traversed the tank at an increased rate. Turtles hauled out onto the occupied platform significantly more often before selecting a basking site where they tended to remain for the duration of the trial. 22615: Distribution and habitat preference are of paramount importance when evaluating management options, including preservation, conservation, relocation, and reintroduction of a species. 22616: Reproductive period, clutch production strategy, size at reproductive maturity, and the development of secondary sex characteristics were investigated in individuals of the Blacknose Shiner, Notropis heterolepis, collected from the glacial lakes region of northeastern Illinois during April through October 2002 and again in 2003. 22617: Male choice of female mates is a potentially important source of variation in mating success within and among populations. Males preferred unparasitized females in paired-female presentations. The preference for unparasitized females was also present during single-female presentations, but the preference was less obvious. During observations on natural courtship patterns, we found parasitized females were courted less often than expected. In addition, unparasitized males courted unparasitized females more often than expected. Correspondingly, parasitized males courted parasitized females more often than expected. It appears that although the effect of A. partiti on preferences of male S. partitus is not as dramatic as on females, this parasite can still play an important role in the reproductive success of females. 22618: In the last year, herpetologists have learned of the establishment on Guam of three new frog species. Of these, the Greenhouse Frog, Eleutherodactylus planirostris, is in some ways the most problematic, as its exclusively terrestrial development will allow it to colonize the entire island. The other two species, Rana cf. nigromaculata and an as yet unidentified treefrog, will remain limited to the southern half of the island, where surface water provides breeding sites. All three constitute an ecological threat in their own right, as well as providing a key food supply for further increasing population densities of the Brown Treesnake, Boiga irregularis. The 10-30 g treefrog is the most worrisome in that regard, as it fills a void in prey size between the current diversity of abundant small (< 6 g) lizards, and a number of introduced mammals (> 35 g). At least one and probably two of the new frog species arrived accidentally via the aquaculture trade. I would be most interested in hearing suggestions from the ichthyological community on how best to reduce the inadvertent transport of frogs in aquaculture stock. The accidental transport of Greenhouse Frogs, possibly as eggs on potted plants, will be particularly difficult to prevent. Populations of all three frog species reached sizes too large to control prior to discovery by authorities. In the case of the Greenhouse Frog, roughly 10,000 people live in the densely colonized area (which previously supported only the giant introduced anuran Bufo marinus). That no citizen deemed the frogs' arrival worthy of reporting to authorities suggests that herpetologists have done an inadequate job in educating residents about the native species living in their midst, and about the hazards of allowing the establishment of exotic species (on Guam!).

22619: In 1996 the first specimens of a remarkable, undescribed siluriform (the "Chiapas catfish") were collected from the Río Usumacinta by the first author. Structurally related features include: narrowing of frontals and parts of sphenotics; a prominent, flattened sphenotic spine carrying infraorbital sensory canal; skull roof lacking prominent sagittal crests or fossae for muscle attachment. 2) Hyomandibula expanded anteriorly as a deep blade formed mostly by dorsoanterior hypertrophy of levator arcus palatini crest (which muscle inserts primarily along its dorsomedial free edge) and hyomandibula pierced by a large foramen for passage of a branch of mandibular nerve to deeper parts of adductor mandibularis muscle. 3) Gas bladder with a pair of prominent diverticula protruding from anterodorsal wall, each diverticulum extending dorsad in front of anterior limb of fourth transverse process, lateral to first centrum and anterior prong of tripus, and posterior to occiput and ossified Baudelot's ligament. 4) Palatine bone greatly foreshortened anterior to its lateral ethmoid condyle; its anterior cartilage mesially continuous with cartilage of lateral ethmoid condyle. 5) Thin anterior extension of lateral ethmoid bone forms hemicylindrical roof over olfactory nerve. 6) "Pseudo-pharyngobranchial bone anterior and medial to first epibranchial. Although superficially similar to ictalurids, the "Chiapas Catfish" differs from them by its autapomorphies plus absence of pelvic fin and girdle specializations. The "Chiapas Catfish" shares a nasal barbel with a large group of Old World catfishes plus ictalurids. A phylogenetic analysis using over 250 morphological characters and 82 terminal taxa fails to resolve the systematic position of the "Chiapas Catfish."

22620: Over the past 20 years, relationships among extant crocodylians have been in contention since the results of virtually all molecular studies have contradicted morphological phylogenetic interpretations. 22622: It has been proposed that lizards inhabiting tropical/low altitude areas have better opportunities to grow than those inhabiting temperate/high altitude areas. 22623: The live animal trade may be an important source for the introduction of vertebrate species. 22624: The Rainbow Scorpionfish Scorpaenodes xyris (Jordan and Gibert, 1882) (Scorpaeniformes: Scorpaenidae) is a small cryptic fish distributed on shallow rocky reefs from California to Peru. 22625: Xenopus laevis tadpoles that arrest development and remain as larvae for more than 1 year occasionally occur in laboratory populations. These tadpoles cease development at an early limb bud stage and continue to grow, developing into grossly deformed giants, which average 4 times longer and up to 50 times more massive than normal tadpoles of corresponding stage. Non- transforming giant X. laevis tadpoles lack thyroid glands, and differ in gross morphology and behavior from normal X. laevis tadpoles. Giants have spinal scoliosis; their axial and tail musculature is disproportionately large relative to the rest of their body. Giants are negatively buoyant, and frequently rest on the tank bottom. In most cases their lungs are small and partially solidified, with numerous septa and abundant collagen. Fat bodies are greatly enlarged. Although gonads are not differentiated in normal tadpoles of the same stage, ovaries in giants are well developed and full of eggs. When induced to metamorphose by exogenous thyroid hormone (T3) treatment, giants develop fore-limbs, their head and mouth shape transform, but the tadpoles fail to completely metamorphose; all die at the stage when the tail normally starts resorbing. Neoteny has never been reported in anurans, but the complete gonadal development of these tadpoles brings them as close as any anurans to being truly neotenic. Complete metamorphosis may not be possible in giant tadpoles due to a disproportionate growth and development of tissues and organs. The inability to amplex and possibly mechanical factors that prohibit forceful extrusion of sperm and eggs may hinder both reproduction in giant Xenopus larvae and the evolution of neoteny in anurans in general.

22626: Few studies have estimated demographic rates of terrestrial life stages of amphibians with respect to differences in habitat quality or land use. 22627: Recent ecomorphological studies have shown that the predicted correlations between morphology and ecology on broad taxonomic levels are often obscured when comparing more closely related groups. 22628: Estuaries are heterogenous environments that serve as nursery habitats for a multitude of fishes. 22630: A revised data matrix for early tetrapods, based on more than 100 taxa and more than 350 characters, is used to reconstruct the cladistic relationships among stem amniotes. 22631: The Redfin Shiner, Lythrurus umbratilis, is a wide-ranging species distributed throughout much of the Ohio, Tennessee, Mississippi, Missouri, and a few of the western Gulf Coastal drainages. Two subspecies are currently recognized based on well-defined differences in breeding tuberculation and coloration. In 1980, WC Starnes collected a potentially novel form that lacked all dark fin pigmentation from the upper Ouachita system in Arkansas. Subsequent collecting efforts (in 1994) revealed this form to inhabit the upper reaches of the Ouachita River system above the fall line. Based on fin coloration, apparent intermediates between this form and L. u. cyanocephalus were found along the fall line with only L. u. cyanocephalus occurring below. During the summer of 2003, additional collections were made to intensively sample this region. Tuberculate materials in peak nuptial coloration were sought to aid in determining the attributes and distribution of this new form. Additionally, large samples were collected for genetic sampling and fine-scale tuning of the population dynamics at play in this system. Here, we report the initial genetic findings of the project and directions for further genetic work.

22632: The cottonmouth, Agkistrodon piscivorus is relatively unique among pit vipers due to its generalized diet. It feeds indiscriminately on almost any small vertebrate, including lizards, snakes, fish, frogs, rodents, and birds. Pitvipers evolved a unique set of anatomical and behavioral features to facilitate capture, relocation, and consumption of larger prey. Pit vipers may vary foraging tactics in response to prey type. Prey release following envenomation is presumably beneficial to avoid retaliatory injury from the prey. Retaining prey can also be beneficial if the prey leaves an intermittent chemical trail and will be lost if released. This method of foraging may also be due to the increased time until mortality for ectotherms, such as frogs. In a laboratory study, we evaluated the effect of prey size and prey type on foraging techniques. A. piscivorus held on to mammalian prey that was smaller than 10% of their body mass, but released mammalian prey that was greater than 20% of their body mass. A. piscivorus was also tested to see if prey capture behavior(s) varied between prey types, looking specifically for any differences between 1) endothermic and ectothermic prey and 2) prey that leave an intermittent scent trail and prey that leave a continuous scent trail. Each snake was presented with each of three different prey types; Green Frog, Rana clamitans, lab mouse, Mus musculus, and domestic chicken, Gallus domesticus. The variables that were examined include latency to begin SICS (searching behaviors), time until location of prey, distance prey traveled, time until death of prey.

22633: Female Blanding's turtles in east-central Minnesota were intensively radio-tracked throughout the 2003 nesting season to determine their habitat use and movement patterns during nesting forays. Nesting forays averaged 8.7 days for turtles tracked over the entire duration of the foray. Nests were constructed an average of 203m from the nearest permanent wetland, and 531m from the resident wetland of the female. All females traveled through prairie, pasture, or rural residential areas during nesting forays, and frequently spent nights under dense vegetative cover, as has been reported in other populations. However, females here were also found to make regular use of small ephemeral wetlands, such as isolated potholes and low spots that temporarily flooded after heavy rains. Ninety-one percent of females entered at least one ephemeral wetland, and 37% used two or more such wetlands during nesting forays. Females spent at least part of the day in ephemeral wetlands in 86% of the total days spent on nesting forays. Nesting females may use ephemeral wetlands to escape high ambient temperatures or for intake of water that will be used to soften soil during nest-digging. Ephemeral wetlands may also serve as refuges along travel routes to nest sites. These refuges could make it possible for females to safely increase the duration of their nesting forays, thereby allowing them to both nest farther from their resident wetland, and to wait for optimal nesting conditions. The presence of ephemeral wetlands for use as refuges is expected to be especially important in populations where females travel long distances from their resident wetlands to nest, which is supported by the data from this population. This research suggests that small ephemeral wetlands are an important component of Blanding's turtle nesting habitat in Minnesota. Preservation of these wetlands should be considered when planning management strategies for this species.

22634: The classical evolutionary view that behavior is both a precursor and driver of phenotypic change has been justifiably questioned. The role of behavior in adaptive radiation has been discussed for more than a century, yet evidence for behavior’s capacity to drive significant phenotypic change is surprisingly scarce. Making explicit use of phylogenetic information, we present compelling evidence that behavior can drive phenotypic change and adaptive radiation. We surveyed vertebrates that use a mimetic appendage to attract prey and found extensive convergence in trophic structure and function. Vertebrates as diverse as fishes, frogs, turtles, and snakes show analogous coadapted character complexes associated with ambush predation and extreme macrophagy. Using character mapping techniques and available phylogenies of anglerfishes (Lophiiformes) and snakes (Serpentes), we analyzed evolutionary trends in prey luring and trophic adaptations. Our analyses detected a correlation between prey luring and extreme macrophagy, as well as trends in elaboration of trophic morphology associated with extent of a lineage’s exposure to prey luring. This evidence is particularly clear-cut because the behavior (prey luring—and its associated morphology) is structurally and functionally separate from the morphologies, physiologies, and behaviors being driven; thus, the correlations we detected are not expected without a causal link. Based on these correlations, we suggest that prey luring was a key innovation in the origin and diversification of macrostomate snakes, and a critical factor in the early transition from the basal alethinophidian diet to an adult diet of primarily bulky mammals. Differences in adult and juvenile feeding ecologies are implicated as causal in the evolution of prey luring in snakes.

22635: The global decline in amphibian diversity has become an international environmental problem. While the causes of amphibian declines are diverse, there is evidence that pesticides may play a role. The herbicide Roundup is a globally-common pesticide that is applied across millions of hectares of wetlands and croplands. Conventional wisdom is that Roundup is nonlethal to amphibians, yet it has rarely been tested on amphibians, particularly in North America. Using six species of North American amphibian larvae (Rana sylvatica, R. pipiens, R. clamitans, R. catesbeiana, Bufo americanus and Hyla versicolor), I examined the impact of a globally-common herbicide (Roundup) on tadpole survival in the laboratory. LC50 estimates varied from 0.55 to 2.52 mg of active ingredient (AI)/L, considerably lower than the few previous studies using Roundup (1.7 to 15.5 mg AI/L) on amphibians from other continents. I then assembled communities of tadpoles in more natural outdoor mesocosms (containing different types of soil, which can absorb the pesticide) and simulated a direct overspray of Roundup on a wetland. After 3 wks, Roundup killed 96-100% of larval amphibians (regardless of soil presence). Finally, I exposed three species of juvenile anurans (post-metamorphic) to the terrestrial application of Roundup. After 1 d, Roundup killed 68-86% of juvenile amphibians. These results suggest that Roundup can cause high rates of mortality to both larval and juvenile amphibians.

22636: Theory proposes that speciation will be accelerated in groups where female mate choice is strong. The Goodeinae, a speciose clade of endemic Mexican fishes, provides an opportunity to assess the link between sexual selection and diversification, as the group possesses substantial interspecific variation in body morphology that appears to influence mate choice. A phylogeny constructed with mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase I and control region DNA data suggests a role for vicariance in early radiation, but this pattern is only weakly supported by comparative tests. The role of female mate choice was assessed by quantifying interspecific variation in sexual dimorphism for 25 goodeines using a multivariate measure of total morphological differentiation between the sexes. This method reflects at least part of the sexual dimorphism driven by sexual conflict. Speciation rate is predicted to be higher where sexual dimorphism is greatest as female- biased conflict will accentuate divergence due to limited gene flow. However, comparative analyses failed to support a significant association between sexual dimorphism and speciation rate. Variation in the time course of speciation for the clade was also examined using a similar tree containing 34 extant species. A constant rates model for the growth of this clade was rejected. Instead analyses suggest a decline in the rate of speciation over time. Collectively, these results support the hypothesis of early expansion of the group, perhaps due to an early adaptive radiation influenced by the key innovation of livebearing, or the prevalence of Miocene volcanism on the southern Mexican plateau.

22637: The fish community of the Sinú River (ZDERS), Córdoba, Colombian Caribbean, was evaluated by monthly surveys between November 2000 and December 2002, with the purpose of evaluating the major changes inflicted by the onset of functioning of the Urrá I hydroelectric dam. Surveys where made in seven marshy areas downstream of the dam during high and low river levels. Overall, collections included 4,017 individuals representing 18 orders, 61 families, and 127 species. The analysis of classification and ordination defined three distinct fish communities: freshwater, freshwater-estuarine, and coastal-estuarine. This result is in contrast with a study made by INVEMAR (1999) before Urrá I stated functioning, which only found the formation of two fish communities: freshwater-estuarine and coastal-estuarine. The appearance of a clearly defined freshwater community during the period of this study is reflected by species such as Caquetaia kraussi and Cyphocharax magdalenae , that seemed favored by the environmental disturbance caused by the dam, changing from occasional dwellers to resident species of these marshes. Furthermore, the individuals and species numbers recorded during high water periods showed significant differences between 1998 versus 2001 and 2002; these variations through years can be related with Urrá I functioning, the variations inherent to natural fish’s cycles, and /or fishing pressure in the area of study.

22638: Pupfish are very tolerant of environmental extremes occurring in a wide range of salinities and temperatures. The White Sands Pupfish, Cyprinodon tularosa is no different. This fish occupies four distinct habitats within the Tularosa Basin of South-central New Mexico. Two of the habitats (Lost River and Salt Creek) are riverine systems that have large variations in salinity, With salinities approaching three times that of seawater. Despite high variations in salinity, pupfish occur throughout both systems. Lost River is a small riverine system that is fairly accessible with salinity varying throughout the length of the system. As male pupfish are territorial breeders, it is assumed that larger fish will inhabit areas that maximize fitness. To determine habitat preference of fish, habitat measurements were made in a 4 m2 area surrounding minnow traps, that were set along the length of Lost River. Salinity levels were highly correlated with the median length of fish. As salinity increased the median size of fish decreased, suggesting that low to moderate levels of salinity are preferrred. Although pupfish are fairly tolerant, salinity should not be neglected when selecting potential sites for translocations. Salinity differences can have important direct and indirect effects on pupfish evolution.

22639: Deep coral banks, composed mostly of Lophelia pertusa, occur in scattered patches off the southeastern US in depths of 350-700 m. Fish communities of these banks are poorly known. Also, the affinity of fishes for reef habitat in the deep sea is not well understood. From 2000-2003 we surveyed the fishes of deep coral banks off North Carolina and South Carolina using a research submersible (23 dives) and bottom trawls (15 stations). In addition to documenting species composition, relative abundance, and size structure of fishes on and near the coral habitat, we investigated to what extent various deep sea fishes are obligate (primary) reef fishes. Lophelia coral banks on the continental slope off the southeastern US support a distinct fish assemblage compared to non-coral habitats of similar depths. Thus far, we have identified over 41 fish species on the coral banks. Numerically dominant species observed on this habitat include Beryx decadactylus, Helicolenus dactylopterus, Laemonema melanurum, Hoplostethus occidentalis, Conger oceanicus, and Laemonema barbatulum. Economically important species observed on coral banks include Polyprion americanus (wreckfish) and H. dactylopterus (black-bellied rosefish). Additionally, we have collected and/or observed several poorly known species on the coral banks (e.g., Idiastion kyphos, Physiculus karrerae, Scyliorhinus meadi, and Lophiodes beroe). These fishes may have appeared to be rare because they prefer a habitat that is difficult to sample. Squalus asper, L. melanurum, H. occidentalis, S. meadi, and B. decadactylus appear to be restricted to the coral habitat and should be considered primary reef fishes. Further collections and data analysis will add species to this deep reef assemblage.

22641: Catch data from over 6000 trawl tows were collected in a collaborative program between SMAST and the New Bedford, Massachusetts trawler fleet. 22642: The rapid evolution of Lake Malawi cichlids has made discrimination among these fishes difficult, leaving many species improperly classified or undescribed. The Metriaclima cf. livingstonii complex currently complex consists of four recognized species (Metriaclima elegans, Metriaclima lanisticola, Metriaclima pursus, and Metriaclima livingstonii) and several undescribed allopatric populations. Metriaclima livingstonii was described based on a single specimen whose type locality is unknown. Previous studies by us demonstrated that the M. livingstonii holotype is not representative of any of the known allopatric populations of the M. cf. livingstonii complex. Recent analyses indicate that the M. livingstonii holotype is more similar to M. elegans than to any of the other fishes in this complex and is probably a juvenile. Further complicating the systematics of this group is the issue that although M. elegans is widely distributed through out Lake Malawi the species was insufficiently described based on only one specimen. To resolve the systematics of these fishes we propose a revision of the entire complex including redescriptions of original holotypes and new species descriptions of several allopatric populations previously consolidated together under the name M. livingstonii.
