22643: Mammoth Cave National Park (MCNP) is home to two unique and important natural features. It is the location of the longest cave system in the world and it is dissected by the Green River. The Green River drainage is a region with one of the highest fish species diversities on the continent. The river and the cave systems meet where subterranean rivers emerge on the banks of the Green as springs. This creates a direct aquatic link between the subterranean rivers of the cave and the Green River itself. The history of the subterranean river systems in MCNP is filled with eyewitness reports of various species of surface water (nontroglobitic) fishes. This survey is an attempt to document the occurrence of Green River fish species in the cave system of MCNP. Four sites were selected on three subterranean waterways. These sites, Owl Cave, Echo River, and Dead Sea and River Styx Shallow, were chosen for volume of water and accessibility. Five methods were incorporated into the sampling regime. Passive sampling methods included gillnetting, lighted larval fish traps, and baited minnow traps. Active methods utilized were backpack electrofishing and dipnetting. In combination these methods successfully captured over 200 fishes (mostly larval) representing the following families; Amblyopsidae, Centrarchidae, Clupeidae, Cottidae, Cyprinidae, Atherinidae, Percidae, and Sciaenidae. Fish were captured from three of the four sites, mainly after high water events. The results will be discussed with reference to the hydrology of the cave system and its possible implications for energy and nutrient flow.

22644: We studied habitat use, population biology and movement patterns of the terrestrial, direct- developing frog Eleutherodactylus punctariolus in 4 headwater streams at a mid-elevation site in Central Panama. 22646: We trapped anurans and their predators from eight ponds in eastern Texas on a weekly basis from January 2002 through December 2003. 22647: The species Chaetostoma loborhynchos was described on 1845 based on a single, poorly fixed, specimen collected by J. Von Tschudi from the Tulumayo River, central Peru. 22648: A remarkable diversity of lipophilic alkaloids are present in the skin of poison frogs and toads worldwide. Originally discovered in Neotropical dendrobatid frogs, these alkaloids are now known from mantellid frogs of Madagascar, certain myobatrachid frogs of Australia, and several bufonid toads of South America. These alkaloids appear to be sequestered from a variety of alkaloid-containing arthropods and are presumably active as a passive chemical defense against predation and/or microorganisms. The cardiotonic pumiliotoxins represent a major, widespread, group of alkaloids, which are found in all anurans that are chemically defended by the presence of lipophilic alkaloids. The spiropyrrolizidine alkaloids are found in several poison frogs and toads throughout the tropics worldwide. Identifying an arthropod source for these alkaloids has been a considerable challenge for chemical ecologists. However, an extensive collection of Neotropical forest arthropods has now revealed arthropod sources for these unique alkaloids. Here we report on the presence of pumiliotoxins in formicine ants of the genera Brachymyrmex and Paratrechina as well as the presence of spiropyrrolizidines in millipedes of the genus Rhinotus. Pumiliotoxins and spiropyrrolizidines are major alkaloids in the microsympatric dendrobatid frog, Dendrobates pumilio, and it is likely that these formicine ants and siphonotid millipedes represent dietary sources of these alkaloids. These findings also provide further evidence for the importance of myrmecophagy and alkaloid sequestration in the evolution of aposematic coloration in poison frogs and toads.

22649: The influence of environmental gradients (e.g., altitude, climate, and landcover) on herpetofauna is important for conservation and management. To elucidate species responses to environmental gradients, ordination methods, such as canonical correspondence analysis (CCA), has been widely and successfully used in other taxa, but neglected in herpetological studies. We found a strong geographic gradient in species composition that was correlated with elevation, human population, climate, and landcover. Reptiles and amphibians responded differently to gradients. Reptiles were strongly influenced by landcover (residential, agricultural, and forested area), while amphibians responded to all gradients, landcover, climate, and altitude. Species currently in decline all appeared near the center of the ordination space. They all are typical inhabitants of satoyama landscape (traditional rural areas, comprised of a mosaic of land covers, such as residential areas, agricultural lands, and forests), which are under rapid modification due to recent human activities. I propose that CCA, as well as other ordination methods, should be more commonly applied in herpetofaunal community studies.

22650: The Asian natricine snake Rhabdophis tigrinus possesses a series of paired nuchal glands, which serve a defensive function by releasing a noxious fluid. Several lines of evidence suggest that the active compounds in the fluid may be sequestered from toxic anuran prey, such as toads. Previous morphological studies have revealed that the glands lack an epithelial layer and the cells do not possess the abundant secretory organelles typical of glands. We studied the early development of the vasculature in embryonic Rhabdophis through gross observation of fresh embryos and vascular injections of ink. Morphology of the adult vasculature was revealed by perfusion with Microfil, a fine latex. In gross examination, anterior integumentary vessels appear in the embryo before the nuchal glands are evident. However, the first definitive sign of the glands themselves is the appearance of paired clusters of melanophores in the nuchal region. These melanophores are evident shortly before the integumentary color pattern begins to appear. Nuchal glands of adults exhibit circumferential blood vessels and dense, central capillary beds. Anterior glands are served by branches of the internal carotid artery, whereas more posterior glands are served by the network of integumentary vessels that underlie the dorsal scales. The dense microvasculature of the nuchal glands is consistent with the hypothesis that defensive compounds are delivered to the glands via the circulatory system, rather than being synthesized within the glands themselves.

22651: The Asian Forest Tortoise, Manouria emys, possesses a variety of unique behaviors and characteristics including modification of nesting material construction and guarding of nest mounds. Of terrestrial genera, it is the fourth largest worldwide, largest in Indomalaya and has the largest single clutches. Despite these characters and having been described 160 years ago, it is severely underrepresented in literature, most being redescriptive. A four-week study was initiated to gather data and generally determine the current status of M. emys in Malaysia and Thailand. Objectives were observation of in and ex-situ animals, preserved specimens, food markets, and in-range researcher interviews. Sites visited included Sabah, Malaysian Borneo (Lahad Datu, Tabin Wildlife Reserve, Sepilok, Labuk Bay, and Kota Kinabalu), Peninsular Malaysia (Kuala Lumpur), and Thailand (Kaeng Krachan National Park, and Bangkok). Food markets revealed no M. emys, but availability was offered in Kuala Lumpur on a day’s notice. Researchers were interviewed in Tabin, Sepilok, Kuala Lumpur, and Bangkok. Museum collections were seen in Bangkok but also exist in Kota Kinabalu, and Kuala Lumpur. Ex-situ animals were examined in Sepilok, and Bangkok. Four in-situ tortoises were seen at Tabin, Sepilok, Labuk Bay, and Kaeng Krachan in over 300 man-hours of survey time. In conjunction with the dearth of food market animals, populations may have declined since receiving endangered status in 2000. Cryptic habits may contribute to this, but decreased or disjunct populations make this animal virtually impossible to locate in the wild. Results of this endeavor call into question the validity of data from the single in situ study. 22652: On small, dry Caribbean islands, Cnemidophorus lizards consume primarily a plant diet. 22657: The question of why some animal species feeding on a particular food type become phenotypically specialized, whereas other species with apparently similar diets do not, has plagued evolutionary biologists for many years. Lizards are an ideal group to address this question because there is a growing body of data regarding both natural diets and feeding systems. Nonetheless, there has been no adequate review of this topic since Greene (1982). In this paper I consider some of the general issues relating to the phenotype-diet relationship, emphasizing the cases of myrmecophagy, herbivory and carnivory. Several preliminary conclusions are possible: Phenotype and diet show no predictable association among lizards. As such, the rules governing the relationship between ecological and phenotypic specialization remain unknown and the prediction of diet from form and form from diet is undertaken at considerable risk. One potential problem is that many putative cases of dietary stenophagy might actually reflect inadequate sampling; temporal or geographic variation in diet can lead to cryptic omnivory tending to promote phenotypic generalization over evolutionary time. A second and perhaps more important problem, is the common practice of using taxonomic categories to denote dietary specialization. Use of such categories is based on ecological interests relating energy flow among trophic levels rather than on the selective forces driving phenotypic specialization in consumers. Specialization of the feeding apparatus depends on the mechanical challenges posed by a given food type during each stage of feeding, not on food taxon. The assumption of dietary specialization based on traditional, ecological-taxonomic categories, (e.g., "herbivory" and "myrmecophagy") is, in most cases, unsupported. Evolutionary morphologists should devise new, functional or mechanistic conceptions of "dietary specialization" if they are to relate diet to the functional morphology of feeding and therefore, phenotypic evolution.

22658: When there are unequal numbers of each sex available to mate, the more abundant sex is competitive and the more limited sex is choosy. One such species, Syngnathus scovelli, is polyandrous; females may mate multiply, yet males typically receive eggs from only one female. S. scovelli, is also the most sexually dimorphic of the syngnathids studied to date. Females are typically larger than males and have a silvery bar on each bony ring of the trunk (the barring pattern). However, female competitive behavior in this species has yet to be formally described. I allowed two females to interact in a 20-gallon tank for 1 hour. Interactions often began with lateral displays in which the females swam next to each other, paralleling each other’s movements. Common displays included one female leaning or pushing the trunk of her body toward the other female. This was often combined with a shudder involving violent shaking of the entire body. This temporary ornament enhanced the permanent barring pattern. The female giving the most displays emerged as dominant. 22659: Vertebrates display a broad spectrum of adaptive responses of their digestive system to feeding and fasting. This is exemplified among amphibians and reptiles from species that feed relatively frequently and experience modest fluctuations in intestinal performance to those species that feed infrequently and widely regulate intestinal performance with feeding and fasting. This is apparent for snake species that feed very infrequently in the wild and anurans that estivate for months during the dry season. The proximate mechanisms underlying the regulation of intestinal performance are divided between morphologic and functional responses. In contrast, the response of amphibian and reptilian intestinal nutrient transport to fasting is much more variable, ranging from no change to as much as an 80% decline in mass-specific nutrient uptake. The reduction in microvillar length during fasting, as observed for pythons, undoubtedly contributes to the downregulation of intestinal performance.

22660: In considering the tremendous metabolic response exhibited by pythons during meal digestion and the well-known phenomenon of blood shunting to active tissues, we measured heart rate, cardiac output (summed blood flow through the carotid arteries and dorsal aorta), and blood flow through the superior mesenteric artery and hepatic portal vein of Burmese pythons while fasting, exercising, and digesting. 22663: As so notably demonstrated by Eric Pianka's pioneering studies on desert lizards, research on novel, relatively unstudied systems can provide a broad perspective with which to evaluate the generality of ideas that have been proposed from better-known kinds of organisms and habitats. 22665: The long-term stability and usefulness of a fluid preserved specimen depends on three factors: (1) the quality of initial fixation and preservation; (2) post-preservation processing and handling; and (3) the quality of the storage environment. The amount of care taken with the initial preservation is arguably the most critical factor in determining how useful the specimen will be. To ensure maximum quality, process the specimen as soon as possible after it is collected. Euthanize the specimen quickly and humanely. Keep the time interval between death and fixation or initial preservation as short as possible. Measure chemicals accurately and mix them with distilled or deionized water (if available). The fixative (usually formaldehyde) or preservative (usually ethyl alcohol) must penetrate rapidly into the tissues. Penetration time can be shortened by fixing at warmer temperatures (25-35ºC). If a fixative is not used, the preservative should be introduced by perfusion. Maintain a ratio of at least 1:2 between specimen volume and fixative or preservative volume. Stage specimens from field fixative or preservative to the storage solution by 20% steps of increasing concentration to reduce osmotic shock and to avoid diluting the storage preservative. Maintain a stable temperature and relative humidity in the storage environment and protect specimens from visible light, ultraviolet radiation, and vibrations. A temperature of 65- 70ºF (18-21ºC) and relative humidity at or just below 50% is preferred for the storage of fluid preserved collections. Store specimens in containers that have a good seal between the container and the closure and are impermeable to oxygen and other contaminates. Handle specimens carefully to avoid physical damage, dehydration, and rehydration (for example, do not put alcohol-preserved specimens in water for examination, and do not leave them of out the preservative solution for an extended period of time).

22666: Stormwater retention ponds, designed to mitigate the effects of runoff from impervious surfaces, may provide amphibian habitat, especially given marked global declines in natural wetlands. 22668: Previous work in the southeastern United States has documented that goldstripe darters (Etheostoma parvipinne) commonly occur in small low-gradient streams with shallow water depths and predominately sand substrates. 22671: Fossils provide the most valid calibration data for molecular clock hypotheses, but applications require careful examination of the assumptions and possible failings of paleontological data. 22672: The impacts of nonindigenous species on native ecosystems can be severe, sometimes leading to the extinction of native taxa. Some 70% of individuals were less than 100m away upon recapture but 2% moved 10km or more. The maximum dispersal distance recorded was the maximum extent of the area studied, 35 km, but only two individuals were found to have moved that far. No difference was found between male and female dispersal and no difference was found between adult and juvenile dispersal, in contradiction of expectations based on life- history theory. More juveniles than adults are found dispersing long distances solely for the reason that juveniles are more abundant than adults. Both active dispersal by toads, due to their own movements, and passive dispersal of toads, borne by the currents of the lake, occur at Long Point. Our results indicate that metapopulation structures in Fowler s toads should not emerge unless breeding habitat patches are separated on the order of 10 km from each other and, therefore, Long Point has but one, patchy population of Fowler s toads.

22676: The São Francisco river is the longest one entirely comprised within Brazilian territory. According to recent studies, around 160 freshwater fish species are currently known from that system, with some obviously representing endemic groups. Mentions to genera and species observed in that system and belonging to the gymnotiform families Apteronotidae, Gymnotidae and Sternopygidae are somewhat common in available literature. Conversely, almost nothing is known regarding the occurrence of the Hypopomidae in that basin. Published (i.e., "formal") accounts on this subject are apparently restricted to only two citations, both merely listing the presence of species of Hypopomus Gill in that system (not mentioning any examined specimens or collection sites). Working on a major parcel of all hypopomid material so far collected in the rio São Francisco drainage (middle São Francisco region), we found that it actually does not belong to that genus above. All specimens available to us exhibit an accessory electric organ externally visible laterally on the underside of the head and cheeks (near the opercle region, a unique condition among gymnotiforms). We are aware of additional material showing that same apomorphic feature above, and from other South American drainages (e.g., Amazonas, Essequibo, Orinoco, and Paraná-Paraguay), suggesting a widely distributed monophyletic unit (perhaps a new hypopomid genus). 22677: HerpNET is an international collaboration combining data from 36 institutions in North America. The project consists of: (1) georeferencing (obtaining coordinates for) all unique localities for each of the participating institutions; (2) establishing DiGIR servers at each institution to act as a portal for the institutional data, as well as the data of all other participants; (3) establishing a concise methodology for determining coordinates and error; (4) training all participants in georeferencing methods; (5) training all participants how to install their DiGIR provider and update collection data on their server; (6) facilitating the inclusion of other institutions in the project in the future; and (7) encouraging use of the products of HerpNET, namely the georeferenced museum catalogs, for applications such as predictive modeling of species occurrence, determination of species niches and faunal shifts through time, and field verification of species occurrences. Progress has been made toward these goals. A gazetteer of localities to be georeferenced was made available in early 2004 and includes more than 600,000 unique localities for ≈ 3.7 million specimen records. A website of current georeferencing progress, methods, georeferencing error calculator, and gazetteer of localities can be found at http://herpnet.org. The web pages will be shown during the poster session, along with demonstrations of the georeferencing methods and DiGIR protocols. HerpNET is an innovative project that will revolutionize the ability of the herpetological community to access museum data and localities. By georeferencing many collections in North America and keeping these data up-to-date, we are providing information that is vital for studies on amphibian and reptile biodiversity, conservation, phylogenetics, ecology, and evolution.

22678: Studies of geographic variation within species are important for identifying speciation processes and its causes. Thirty-seven morphological characters from 673 adults were analyzed using Principal Components Analysis. Many traits varied within the Eastern, Western and Middle groups, as well as among these groups. Mensural traits were highly variable among regions, and there was only a slight trend in body size to be higher in the north. Other characters that showed clinal variation were ventral scale counts, which increased with decreasing longitude, and the number of scales before the supraoculars, which were higher in the east. Variation in non-mensural data was better explained along a longitudinal cline, possibly due to environmental differences. Snakes across all biogeographic regions ate mammals and reptiles and there were no ontogenetic dietary shifts from ectothermic to endothermic prey. For reproductive analyses, 155 females showed reproductive activity between April and October. No clinal trends exist in timing of reproduction, clutch size or frequency of reproduction among regions. Crotalus atrox may truly be a generalist species. It seems to vary little across its range in terms of prey eaten, morphological traits or reproductive output. Crotalus atrox represents a species with a large geographic range size with phenotypic variation throughout its range, making it a good model organism for further studies of environmental effects and biogeographical processes across western North America.

22680: This work demonstrates that the evolution of herbivory in lizards (Sauria, Lacertilia) has repeatedly produced convergent skull morphologies. Herbivory has evolved multiple times within lizards, but the morphological consequences of this dietary strategy have not been studied quantitatively among multiple groups. Functionally relevant landmarks were digitized on 1030 lizard skulls and lower jaws, and were used to construct two multidimensional morphospaces of lizard skull and lower jaw shape. The coordinates of individual lizards in these spaces were used to test hypotheses of convergence within herbivorous members of 8 families. Deviations of herbivores away from their carnivorous sister groups were calculated, and patterns of convergent or parallel change were described. For the lower jaw morphospace, predictions were made concerning the directions in which herbivores should deviate from their carnivorous relatives. Specifically, as herbivores do not need to pursue and capture prey, but do need to remove pieces of tough plant material, herbivores are expected to have jaw lever systems with a higher mechanical advantage (MA) than their carnivorous relatives. Results indicate that the evolution of herbivory has caused an interesting pattern of convergence among herbivorous lizards. Although herbivores have not evolved to occupy the same area of morphospace, they do show deviations away from carnivores in the direction predicted by the MA model. This study supports earlier hypotheses concerning the convergent morphologies of certain herbivorous lizards, and it extends the results to families whose herbivorous members did not appear to show specialized, convergent morphologies. It also demonstrates that the integration of biomechanical models and geometric morphometrics provides powerful techniques to develop and test hypotheses concerning the evolution of vertebrate feeding systems.

22683: The Bathymasteridae is a small family of bottom-dwelling marine fishes endemic to the North Pacific. 22684: The two sources of calcium available to developing embryos of oviparous reptiles are the yolk and eggshell. In domestic chickens, the mechanism of calcium transport of the yolk sac differs from the chorioallantoic membrane. Expression of calbindin D28K is correlated developmentally with calcium transporting activity of the yolk sac membrane, but calbindin D28K is not expressed in the chorioallantoic membrane. The mechanism of calcium mobilization to embryos has not been studied in other oviparous amniotes. High calbindin D28K expression was consistently observed in samples of yolk sac and chorioallantois from late stage embryos (Zehr stages 36-37). We occasionally observed high expression in samples of chorioallantois from earlier stages (27-35) but for most of these samples expression was greatly reduced. Furthermore, we conclude that calbindin D28K expression is developmentally regulated and increases during later embryonic stages when there is greater demand for calcium for myogenesis and bone mineralization. 22695: The skeleton of the pectoral fins of skates and rays consists of a series of radially oriented cartilaginous fin rays emanating from the modified pectoral girdle. 22696: Lake Pontchartrain is a large, (164,000 hectares) oligohaline estuary that maintains an average, year-round salinity of 4ppt. 22697: Australian carphodactyline geckos comprise two main lineages adapted to markedly different habitats. The clade comprising the genus Nephrurus occupies dry forest and arid regions across the interior of Australia, whereas the clade comprised of the genera Carphodactylus, Orraya, Saltuarius and Phyllurus occupy mesic vine scrub to rainforest habitats along the eastern margins of the continent. Molecular phylogenetic analyses reveal that the rate of lineage accumulation through time is roughly equivalent in both the desert and rainforest clades, suggesting that diversification in both groups was driven by a shared, external forcing factor. The great age of the carphodactyline lineage is consistent with a Gondwanan origin. The gradual aridification of Australia as it drifted northward from Gondwana may have been the driving factor in the diversification of both the desert and rainforest lineages, the first through increasing ecological opportunity as the variety and extent of arid habitats increased, and the second as a result of climate-driven habitat fragmentation and compositional changes. 22698: The Western Fox Snake (Elaphe vulpina vulpina) is endangered in the state of Missouri, occupying only the northern corners of the state. 22699: Sexual conflict is a ubiquitous feature in animal systems. One commonly explored conflict is over mating rate. Because the optimal mating rate for males is often higher than that for females, particularly in polygamous systems where sperm competition is intense, potential exists for conflict over mating rate when mating is costly. I tested whether there were fitness consequences of high mating rates to females and if intrasexual aggression between males carried a cost in the mosquitofish Gambusia affinis by placing fish in different sex ratio treatments. While mating rate from the female perspective increased as treatments became more male-biased, reproductive success and growth rate actually decreased in female-biased treatments. This is evidence for female-density dependence, which may be an important factor in determining fitness in natural populations regardless of potential costs of male harassment. Male condition and survival was not different between treatments despite significant differences in mating rate and intrasexual aggression.

22702: Models of stream fish population dynamics and assemblage structure are often based on physical habitat conditions at the reach scale (approximately 100 m or fewer of stream). 22703: Habitat alteration is a major cause for amphibian population declines. Pond breeding amphibians are especially vulnerable as they use both aquatic and terrestrial habitats. However, to understand how these species are affected by habitat modification, we must first understand their spatial population structure in areas with minimal human impact. Using microsatellite DNA markers, I examined the genetic structure of a pond breeding amphibian, the Tiger Salamander (Ambystoma tigrinum), across the northern range of Yellowstone National Park. We sampled 11 ponds, with between-site distances ranging from 523 meters to 53 kilometers. There is significant genetic structuring across the area, with pond populations showing genetic differentiation at a scale as small as 1 kilometer. There was also a significant isolation by distance pattern across the entire area. However, genetic distances between some of the ponds deviated from this trend. This is best demonstrated by salamanders from three ponds within 3 km of each other that had a higher degree of differentiation than would be expected by distance alone. These sites are found in the driest part of the study area and are characterized by a large percentage of neotenic individuals, both of which probably contribute to the increased genetic isolation of individuals in these ponds. Overall, it appears that while distance is a primary factor contributing to genetic structure in this study, gene flow between nearby ponds can also be strongly influenced by landscape and ecological factors.

22704: Advances in freshwater turtle population dynamics have lagged well behind the understanding of the population ecology of other taxa (e.g., mammals), primarily because turtles are long-lived. However, despite abundant estimates of common demographic parameters (e.g., survival and fecundity), the dynamics of most populations are not understood because studies are rarely comparative or manipulative. Hence conservation has primarily relied on demographic modeling to determine population status. However, The resilience of a population is dependent on density dependent effects, which have never been estimated in turtles. For example, nest predation is high and many populations may have compensated through increased adult survival. A possible increase of juvenile survival from headstarting programs may actually be countered by a reduction in fecundity or survival in other stages. Thus understanding the dynamics of a population is critical to evaluate relevant management options. In this talk, I evaluate the population dynamics and impact of foxes on Australian freshwater turtle populations through a large-scale reduction of foxes across multiple populations. Some species are more susceptible to predation because of their life history strategies. Nest predation by introduced red foxes on populations of Australian freshwater turtles is a major source of mortality, but foxes also destroy a proportion of nesting adult Emydura macquarii each year; however there appears to be no density dependent compensation in adult survival and foxes potentially regulate these populations. Emydura macquarii populations have low productivity and rely on a standing crop of turtles for population maintenance, whereas a sympatric species, Chelodina expansa, has relatively more juveniles in the population and is less reliant on adult survival. Potential management options are also evaluated.

22705: Temperature dependent sex determination (TSD) has evolved independently in many taxa. 22706: Demography is an important part of the natural history of any species. In particular, age- structured data is valuable in determining population statistics, such as survival rates. Unfortunately, it is often difficult to determine precise ages of individuals. Raising specimens in captivity presents problems, namely unnatural growth. Likewise, because of logistic concerns, mark-recapture studies seldom provide accurate age. Bone of reptiles and amphibians living in seasonal climates typically grows in layers. As such, skeletochronology has been used to estimate age in many species of temperate reptiles and amphibians. Lizards from Asia, South America, and Africa have been studied. Analysis of bones, such as phalanges and distal caudal vertebrae, is particularly useful because animals need not be sacrificed. We used skeletochronology on phalanges of three species of temperate North American lizards: Texas Horned Lizard (Phrynosoma cornutum); Texas Spotted Whiptail (Cnemidophorus gularis); and Eastern Collared Lizard (Crotaphytus collaris). We attempted to estimate ages for individuals and thereby provide an age structure for each population studied. These data can then be used to estimate growth and survival rates. For example, preliminary results from eastern collared lizard phalanges reveal an average age of 1.6 years (range 0-6) in the studied populations with an annual survival rate of 51% (for ages 1-6). Phalanges collected from animals recaptured in subsequent years were used to validate the skeletochronological technique. Although skeletochronology is extremely time- consuming and requires precision, we feel that it can be a useful demographic tool. Additional research is needed to further refine the technique of skeletochronology on various species of temperate North American lizards, particularly to validate the traditional assumption of one annulus per year for different populations.

22710: Adaptations of males and females to their respective reproductive roles may lead to sexual size dimorphism (SSD) in both animals and plants. When species are compared within a monophyletic clade, SSD is frequently found to vary with body size. This allometry is detected as a slope > 1 for a model II regression of male size on female size if SSD is important, whereas a slope = 1 is detected for isometric patterns of body sizes between males and females. In studies where there is allometry for SSD, the slope of the regression most frequently exceeds 1. This indicates that SSD increases with size where males are the larger sex, but decreases with size where females are the larger sex, a trend formalized as Rensch's Rule. Past reviews on Rensch's Rule claim that allometry for sexual size dimorphism does not exist for Iguanid lizards. Recent advances in iguanid systematics, however, show that lizards used in past studies belong to genera from a large number of families, many of which differ in life histories and mating systems. Thus, past studies may have based conclusions on groups of lizards that are not appropriate units to assess patterns of size dimorphism. Here, I analyze size dimorphism in 20 species of mainland Norops lizards (beta-anoles), by measuring large numbers of preserved specimens. Regression of male size on female size in mainland anoles yields a slope of regression = 1.15, and is significantly different from 1 (p < 0.05). 22713: Three members of the Etheostoma variatum species group, Etheostoma kanawhae, Etheostoma osburni and E. variatum have parapatric distributions in the Kanawha/New River drainage. 22714: Recent studies provide evidence that ecological factors play a role in sympatric speciation. 22716: In most rattlesnake species, adult males are heavier and longer in snout-vent length (SVL) than females. This sexual size dimorphism (SSD) is thought to be the result of sexual selection for large males, since male rattlesnakes fight for access to females. Another hypothesis is that it is beneficial for females to be smaller than males because small females have low metabolic costs of maintenance, allowing them to accumulate energy stores rapidly and reproduce frequently. Alternatively, SSD may be the result of phenotypic plasticity rather than natural selection, with females growing more slowly than males because they have higher energetic costs of reproduction, leaving less energy available for growth. Identification of the proximate, physiological mechanism responsible for SSD would help elucidate the evolutionary and ecological significance of SSD in rattlesnakes. I have conducted a series of experiments to understand how male western diamond-backed rattlesnakes (Crotalus atrox) become larger than females. Male neonates are slightly larger than females, but this difference does not account for the extreme difference in size observed in adult snakes. Testosterone does not appear to stimulate growth in male C. atrox, as it does in many other vertebrates, as castrated free-ranging males grow at the same rate as sham-operated males. Males and females raised on controlled diets in the laboratory grow at the same rates and never diverge in size, with both sexes growing to sizes much in excess of free-ranging snakes. Similarly, supplementation of the diets of free-ranging females leads to dramatic increases in growth. It therefore appears that SSD in C. atrox is the result of phenotypic plasticity, since females are capable of growing to male-like sizes. 22717: We studied the reproductive ecology of a population of western diamond-backed rattlesnakes (Crotalus atrox) in south-central Arizona for four years using radiotelemetry and mark-recapture. Snakes mate in the spring and fall, females undergo vitellogenesis in the spring, ovulate in the early summer, and give birth in the late summer. Variation in levels of steroid hormones over the female reproductive cycle is similar to that in other vertebrates, with estradiol and testosterone elevated during vitellogenesis, and progesterone and corticosterone elevated during gestation. In males, testosterone is elevated during the spring and fall mating periods, and corticosterone levels do not vary seasonally. Females give birth at most every three years, and steroid hormone levels are low in non-reproductive years. Litter sizes range from 2 to 7 neonates (mean = 4.5). There is no relationship between maternal snout-vent length (SVL) and litter size, number of neonates, or mean neonate SVL or mass. The sex ratio of the neonates is approximately 2:1 male:female, and male neonates are longer in SVL and heavier than female neonates. However, this sex difference does not become especially pronounced until snakes grow to approximately 70-75 cm SVL, the size at which sexual maturity is attained in this population. Adult snakes are sexually dimorphic in size, with males growing faster and attaining larger sizes than females.

22718: Although it is now recognized that mutualisms are common and can have stable populations, the forces controlling their persistence are poorly understood. To elucidate empirically the mechanisms that contribute to the stability of an obligate, marine mutualism involving gobies and shrimp on a coral reef, goby densities were perturbed positively and negatively, and it was determined whether population densities returned to pre-manipulation levels. Mutualistic gobies and shrimp are common on coral reefs worldwide and interact as follows: shrimp construct burrows in which both gobies and shrimp reside, and gobies warn shrimp of predators through touch-based signals. Goby densities did not change following goby addition because gobies competed intraspecifically for burrows constructed by shrimp, and large gobies excluded smaller individuals from the burrows. The impact of goby removal on population dynamics was explored through a correlative survey and a direct manipulation of the density of predators. Results of both indicated that goby mortality was greater in locations with high densities of predators. Because gobies have demographically open populations, however, immigrants rapidly replaced individuals that were killed, thus producing no relationship between overall goby and predator densities, but a lower proportion of large gobies and a higher proportion of gobies paired with relatively large shrimp in locations where predators were copious. Hence, in the goby-shrimp mutualism population expansion is prevented through intraspecific competition, whereas immigration buffers the system from extinction.

22719: Tree canopy closure over breeding ponds can affect growth and survival of tadpoles within ponds, and may mediate competitive interactions among species. I conducted two experiments to test whether canopy closure may have contributed to the decline of dusky gopher frogs (Rana sevosa) but allowed the persistence of southern leopard frogs (R. sphenocephala). The response of both species to canopy closure was explored in single and mixed (1:1) species experimental units of identical tadpole density. An experiment using aquatic enclosures in temporary ponds showed that growth of tadpoles of both species was reduced by canopy closure (~20% for both species). Survival of R. sevosa tadpoles was higher in mixed species enclosures than in single species enclosures. In a complementary experiment using artificial ponds, R. sevosa had lower survival to metamorphosis in shaded ponds, whereas R. sphenocephala exhibited reduced size at metamorphosis when shaded. These studies suggest that pond canopy closure, but not larval competition with R. sphenocephala, may be a contributing factor to the decline of the Dusky Gopher Frog. Additionally, the results suggest that the relative ability of a species to respond to habitat change may contribute to the rarity or commonness of that species in altered environments.

22720: Analysis of variance results showed significant differences in measurements on 71 specimens of Aphredoderus sayanus comparing standard length (F = 21.91, P < 0.0001), maximum depth (F = 8.44, P = 0.006), and standard length to body depth ratio (F = 9.11, P = 0.004), indicating that this fish is sexually dimorphic with females being larger and more full-bodied than males. In laboratory observations, a pair of A. sayanuscreated a nest and successfully spawned, which strengthens the argument that this fish might not be a branchial brooder but instead might be a nest builder with the female releasing adhesive eggs in the proximity of the nest. On three separate daytime occasions, A. sayanusventured outside its refuge approximately to the point that only its head and anus were exposed, defecated, and then backed into its refuge. The jugular position of the anus might allow adult A. sayanus to partially leave its refuges to defecate to avoid altering water quality and without fully exposing itself to predators; this unique defecation behavior might explain the evolutionary reason for the position of the anus in adult A. sayanus.

22721: Many studies have assessed effects of large dams on fishes and benthic invertebrates, but few have examined effects of lowhead dams. We compared fishes, benthic invertebrates, habitat, and physicochemistry monthly from November 2000 to October 2001 at eight gravel bar sites centered around two lowhead dams on the Neosho River, Lyon County, Kansas, including a reference site and a treatment site upstream and downstream from each dam. Multivariate analysis of variance indicated site type differences for habitat, and benthic invertebrate and fish abundance, but not physicochemistry. Compared to reference sites, upstream treatment sites were deeper with slower velocity, downstream treatment sites were shallower with faster velocity, and both treatment site types had greater substrate compaction. Benthic invertebrate abundance was lower at downstream treatment sites than at other site types, and treatment sites had lower %EPT. We found more fish in downstream reference sites and fewer in treatment and upstream reference sites. Fish species richness did not differ by site type, but abundance of the federally-listed (threatened) Neosho Madtom, Noturus placidus, was significantly lower immediately upstream and downstream from dams compared to reference sites, whereas abundances of Suckermouth Minnow, Phenacobius mirabilis, Orangethroat Darter, Etheostoma spectabile, and Slenderhead Darter, Percina phoxocephala, were higher in downstream treatment areas than reference sites. The apparent effects of these lowhead dams on fish and benthic invertebrate assemblages were similar to those reported for larger dams.

22722: In order to study patterns of large snake species movement in a mostly natural area, individuals of the Copperhead (Agkistrodon contortrix) were studied in the Land Between the Lakes National Recreation Area (LBL). LBL is a 170,000-acre federally protected area between Kentucky Lake and Lake Barkley in Western Kentucky and Tennessee. On a typical night of road cruising, over 60 percent of the snakes captured are copperheads and because of its undisturbed nature this area was an excellent source of baseline population data for this species. Specimens were observed by road cruising between dusk and dawn. For each date of collection, start time, ending time, temperature, rainfall, wind, humidity, barometric pressure, sun and moon rise, sun and moon set, and moon illumination were recorded. For each point of observation, time of capture, location, status (alive on road (AOR) or dead on road (DOR)), sex, recapture, UTM points, direction traveled, scale clip number, snout-vent length, total length, and release date and time were recorded. At each point of capture, Global Positioning System Universal Transverse Mercator coordinates were recorded. Coordinates for each month period (April through October) were uploaded and plotted on maps using ArcInfo and ArcView software. One-kilometer circular buffer zones were then centered around each point of capture. Digital coverages of soil and vegetation, and digital elevation models were then used to create a database showing the percentages of each within the buffer zones. Analyses indicate that there are habitat type preferences and seasonal differences in habitat in which they are found. The average daily temperature on capture nights was significantly higher than the monthly average in most months. Males and females exhibit different frequencies of movements, as well as juveniles. Dry oak forest and dry oak mesic forest were the most predominant forest types within the buffer zones for each month. There were however, significant differences in within the vegetation from month to month. Soils type at collection sites showed much variation from month to month, while degree of slope showed no significant variation. Slope aspect had no significance from month to month, but within months, the preference leaned toward south and north facing slopes.

22723: The California sheephead, Semicossyphus pulcher (Labridae), is a temperate, rocky-reef/kelp-bed fish that is sought by recreational and commercial fishermen. No-take marine reserves may be an effective management strategy that could protect stocks, but first, it is necessary to determine the movement patterns and site fidelity of this fish. We have used short-term acoustic tracking to effectively ascertain daily fine-scale movement patterns and home range of sheephead; however, this method was not sufficient to determine long-term stability of their home ranges or seasonal movements. Therefore, 16 additional adult (24 to 36 cm SL) sheephead were fitted with long- term (≈1 yr) transmitters and their presence and movement patterns in the Catalina Marine Science Center Marine Life Reserve were monitored by an automated acoustic receiver array. Our short-term tracking has shown that sheephead revisit locations from day to day and had relatively small home ranges (>82,000 m2). The long-term acoustic monitoring data confirms that these sheephead generally have a high degree of fidelity to the areas of the reserve, spending >92% of their days within the reserve area, with most fish utilizing a core area encompassing 2 to 3 monitors (<600 m linear distance). However, these fish showed some variability in area use between months, exhibiting periods of expansion in their range between December and March (non-spawning period), with fish visiting areas previously unutilized. In some cases these expanded movements resulted in the fish crossing the reserve boundary for an extended period or leaving the reserve permanently, potentially exposing the fish to capture. These types of movements may not be revealed in standard tag and recapture studies and should be considered in designing marine reserves.

22724: Amphibian species are declining in many locations around the world, and these declines may serve as warnings of ecosystem imbalances. The Southern High Plains (SHP), a highly fragmented portion of the shortgrass prairie, is home to several species of amphibians. These amphibians breed in playa wetlands, sites that serve as the primary water source for many wildlife species of the SHP. Playas surrounded by cropland often have reduced hydroperiods due to sedimentation. This can affect the species diversity and morphological development of amphibians. Information regarding amphibians that breed in playas is scarce. Because most playas are highly modified by agriculture, our main goal is to study the influence of land use (cropland and grassland) on the survival, population size, and population structure of the Plains Spadefoot Spea bombifrons, New Mexico Spadefoot S. multiplicata, and the Barred Tiger Salamander Ambystoma tigrinum mavortium in larval and terrestrial life stages. We selected 12 playas as study sites, 6 surrounded by cropland and 6 surrounded by native grass. We captured terrestrial forms of amphibians using the pitfall/drift fence technique, and aquatic forms by seining and use of minnow traps. During 2003, we marked amphibians by toe-clipping cohorts of metamorphs uniquely by date and location and by marking recaptures uniquely with elastomer fluorescent ink. Results from the first field season are currently under investigation.

22725: Amphibian embryos face a variety of biotic and abiotic risks, which may affect development and hatching timing as well as survival. Eggs laid near the air-water interface in sites where water level fluctuates may be exposed to two sets of risks, those in both the aerial and aquatic environments. One such species is the common neotropical treefrog Hyla ebraccata which deposits eggs on low vegetation above seasonal ponds. To assess which risks impose the most mortality and potentially the strongest selection pressures on H. ebraccata eggs, I monitored 150 clutches at two ponds in Panama. Total embryo mortality was 65%, mainly due to ant and wasp predation and desiccation. Many clutches were also flooded by rising pond water. Submergence during development kills developing eggs of some other leaf-breeding frogs, but experimentally flooded H. ebraccata embryos developed normally. Experimental dehydration delayed hatching by an average of 10% of the embryonic period. Field observations and pilot experiments also suggest that partially dehydrated clutches are at higher risk of predation. Because desiccation is a major direct and possibly indirect cause of death, flooding may offer hydration benefits. However, H. ebraccata often co-occurs with fish that can be voracious predators on submerged eggs. Thus, it appears that multiple biotic and abiotic factors in both arboreal and aquatic environments interact in complex ways to determine the survival of Hyla ebraccata embryos.

22726: The global population structure of thresher sharks (Alopias pelagicus, A. superciliosus, and A. vulpinus) is virtually unknown. Thresher sharks are taken worldwide both by directed commercial fisheries and as bycatch in tuna and billfish fisheries. Recent analysis of logbook data for the U.S. pelagic longline fleets targeting swordfish and tunas in the Northwest Atlantic indicates that catches of thresher sharks have declined by 80% since 1986, a trend that may reflect their global status. Effective conservation and management strategies for pelagic sharks require a fundamental understanding of their life histories, including population structure. If thresher shark populations are genetically distinct, management guidelines aimed at large geographic areas could be inappropriate, perhaps leading to the permanent loss of regional populations and decreasing their genetic diversity and evolutionary potential. Tissue samples of A. pelagicus, A. superciliosus, and A. vulpinus have been collected from the Northeast Pacific (N = 13,0,32), Central Pacific (N = 0,16,0), Northwest Pacific (N = 3,3,0), Southeast Pacific (N = 21,19,0), Southwest Pacific (N = 0,0,5), Northwest Atlantic (N = 0,15,15), Northeast Atlantic (N = 0,0,6), and Indian (N = 0,1,0) Oceans. We are using mitochondrial DNA control region sequences to quantify the degree of genetic relatedness among geographically disjunct populations of thresher sharks. In addition, DNA sequences from the cytochrome b gene are being used to confirm species identifications of the samples collected. Results will be presented in the context of thresher shark conservation and management.

22727: In this study we used natural stable isotopes (13C and 15N) to assess spatial and temporal variability in dietary habits of fishes within Lake Pontchartrain, an oligohaline estuary in southeastern Louisiana. To ascertain energy resources supporting fisheries production among various habitats within the Lake Pontchartrain Basin, we sampled sources of organic matter (phytoplankton, seagrass, Spartina sp., epiphytes, detritus), zooplankton, bivalves, crustaceans, and fishes at three sites (western, northeastern, eastern) along an estuarine gradient (from oligohaline to euhaline habitats) which correspond with the primary migration route of fisheries species that are recreationally, commercially, and ecologically important. Stable isotope signatures of organisms collected along the estuarine gradient were significantly different. Organic matter collected from the western portion of the estuary was primarily derived from freshwater-based food webs, while organisms collected from the eastern inlet were largely reliant on marine system productivity. Similarly, isotopic signatures from the northeastern sample site were dominated by marine sources of organic matter and generated significantly shorter food chains, possibly indicative of seagrass communities within this region. Number of energy resources differed along the estuarine gradient as the western site was dominated by a combination of freshwater phytoplankton and detritus based food webs with a small contribution from marine phytoplankton during the summer months. Correspondingly, a mixture of detritus and marine phytoplankton dominated the northeastern sites, while the eastern site was driven by marine phytoplankton. Summer food webs in all three regions were relatively stable at all trophic levels while winter food webs were marked by exceptionally high variability, possibly indicating significant differences in the availability of seasonally based consumer resources. Results from this study indicate that fisheries species within this oligohaline estuary rely upon various energy resources across temporal and spatial scales. Further, the relative importance of each estuarine sub-habitat to key fisheries species will be examined.

22728: The nine gobioid families contain more than 2100 species of small fishes, found worldwide in a variety of habitats. Four of these families have traditionally been considered basal, with less extreme manifestation of the morphological reduction that is common among gobioids. Basal gobioids are generally found in fresh or brackish water, and are most numerous in the Old World tropics. We use DNA sequence data from the mitochondrial ND1, ND2, COI and Cytb genes to hypothesize relationships among basal gobioids, and to evaluate the placement of various possible outgroups to Gobioidei. Our hypothesis indicates the presence of two radiations within basal gobioids, one in the West Pacific and Asia, and a second, larger radiation that includes taxa found in the Indo-Pacific, Madagascar, Africa, and the New World. We also consider the divergence of several geminate species pairs across the Isthmus of Panama.

22729: The mode and effectiveness of signals greatly depends on the environmental conditions and activity patterns of the organism. Visual cues are frequently involved in social interactions, although in nocturnal species, chemical cues can be more important. Multiple cues, however, sometimes increase the accuracy and efficiency of communication. Little is known about the mode of communication and association preference of the San Marcos Salamander, Eurycea nana. Therefore, we examined association preferences of males and females based on (1) chemical cues, (2) visual cues, and (3) chemical & visual cues when simultaneously exposed to one individual of each sex. Males and females significantly preferred to associate with the chemical and chemical & visual cues of the opposite sex. Chemical cues were sufficient to elicit a response, as the additional visual cues did not significantly increase the strength of preference for the opposite sex. We further tested male association preference for the chemical & visual cues of gravid versus non-gravid females. We found that males showed no significant preference for either female. These results suggest that although chemosensory communication is sufficient to distinguish between the sexes, the ability of males to discriminate between females of different gravidity states may require an alternate sensory modality, for example tactile interactions. Additionally, association preference can affect the distribution and cohabitation patterns of salamanders. We tested whether salamanders prefer to cohabit in intersexual or intrasexual pairs under artificial shelters rather than reside alone for 20 days. Female pairs and intersexual pairs were found cohabiting more often than expected from random, whereas pairs of males were found more often apart than cohabiting. These results demonstrate that E. nana is probably not territorial and prefers to cohabit. Male preference to stay apart from other males, however, suggests a non-aggressive tactic to reduce competition.

22730: Observations on the occurrence, variation, and taxonomic distribution of odontodes and other features of the epidermis were made using scanning electron microscopy. Differences in the size, shape, and distribution of oral papillae and taste buds between Loricaria and other related genera in Loricariini are illustrated. These differences may be related, at least in part, to different feeding modes (i.e., scraping algae vs. seed-eating) and habitat occurrences. Type I odontodes were present on the surfaces of the leading edges of paired and median fins, as well as the elongate filamentous ray of the caudal fin in all species examined. Observed differences in the structure of odontodes and other epidermal features may have some taxonomic utility and provide new insights into phylogenetic relationships among taxa within Loricariini.

22731: The Illinois Chorus Frog (ICF) is a fossorial hylid with a highly fragmented distribution limited to a few isolated populations in Illinois, the Missouri bootheel, and extreme northeastern Arkansas. Habitat modification for agriculture, including precision land leveling, and environmental stochastic factors have resulted in significant population decline and range contraction for the ICF in Arkansas. Status and distribution surveys conducted in 1987 and 1992 indicated an ICF range of approximately 59 km2. A 2002 survey indicated that ICF range had contracted to a maximum of 39 km2. Due to the highly fragmentary nature of ICF populations, the population structure of the ICF has been referred to as a metapopulation; however, extinction events greatly outnumber colonization events. During the 2003 breeding seeason, DNA samples were collected from adult ICFs in six breeding populations. Due to a lack of rainfall after breeding, no recruitment of ICF larvae occurred in these six populations, and only one other breeding population was discovered during the 2003 breeding season. ICF taxonomy is also currently in question. At present I am conducting molecular genetic techniques, allozyme and amplified fragment length polymorphism analyses, that should clarify the taxonomic issue and provide insight into the degree of genetic diversity within each breeding population and among populations of ICFs and Strecker's chorus frogs (P. s. streckeri).

22732: Human alteration of river ecosystems is an enormous concern worldwide. Our study is focused in the Middle Rio Grande (MRG) of New Mexico, which has been severely altered since the early 1900s. Our aim was to document present conditions and reconstruct past conditions of the Rio Grande aquatic food web to understand how hydrologic alteration has affected ecosystem processes. We used stable isotopes to document the current food web of the MRG and then compared these to isotope signatures obtained from museum-preserved fish specimens collected over the last six decades. Preliminary analysis of carbon isotopes indicated that contemporary fishes gain organic carbon from a variety of sources including algal production, from downstream transport of nutrients, and perhaps from emergent macrophytes and riparian vegetation in adjacent floodplain habitats. Organic carbon in the historical food web appears to have been predominately derived from algal production. Interpretation of nitrogen isotope signatures is more complicated because of difficulty in establishing local baselines, but we discuss longitudinal and temporal patterns of variability in nitrogen signatures. Finally, we discuss some potentials and pitfalls of using museum-preserved materials to evaluate historical food webs.

22733: One key question in biogeography is whether organisms with similar distributions have similar biogeographic histories. Models of cladistic biogeography indicate this should be the case, but the question remains to be tested for most groups. The genus Craterocephalus (Atherinidae, silversides or hardyheads) is largely restricted to freshwater environments in Australian and New Guinea. Craterocephalus currently contains 24 described species, which can be divided into four morphological groups, C. eyresii (10 spp.), C. stercusmuscarum (9 spp.), C. honoriae (4 spp., all marine), and C. stramineus (1 sp.). The C. eyresii and C. stercusmuscarum groups are both widespread in northern Australia and species from these two groups often occur sympatrically. Thus, the sympatric ranges of Australian Craterocephalus species provide an ideal test of cladistic biogeography. To examine the hypothesis that organisms with similar ranges should have similar biogeographic histories, each Australian species, including multiple populations, was sequenced for the mitochondrial cytochrome b gene. A subset of samples were also sequenced for the nuclear S7, RAG1, and RAG2 genes to provide an alternative test of relationships and to increase support for deeper nodes. Results support the existence of the four morphological groups with the following relationships among them: (eyresii (honoriae (stramineus (stercusmuscarum)))). Within the sympatric C. eyresii and C. stercusmuscarum groups there was little overlap in biogeographic patterns, indicating they share almost no common biogeographic history. The results suggest the two groups achieved their current distributions at different times, with the C. eyresii group being older than the C. stercusmuscarum group. Thus, each group has likely been influenced by different biogeographic processes. These results refute the hypothesis that common distribution indicates common biogeographic history.

22734: Solea (Pleuronectiformes; Soleidae) is a genus containing species of considerable commercial importance (Solea Solea, Solea senegalensis). 22735: Male-male combat is widespread among snakes and has been documented in numerous pitvipers. Among rattlesnakes, the behavior has frequently been reported in the genus Crotalus; however, within the genus Sistrurus, fewer reports exist and all are from captive snakes. Male-male combat has been observed in captive Sistrurus catenatus catenatus, but has not been documented in he field. In August 2003, while radio tracking a male Sistrurus catenatus catenatus along the Upper Wapsipinicon River in northeastern Iowa, the radio-tagged male was found in a combat dance with a previously unknown male. The behavior was observed for 55 minutes during which time the snakes were in constant contact. Rapid tongue flicking occurred during the entire time the snakes were in contact and no rattling or biting occurred during the behavior. When compared to the display postures and topping sequence described for Sistrurus miliarius, several similarities were found, specifically; 1) Displaying with the anterior portion of the body elevated and almost always in an S-shape and laterally swaying to gain superior position, 2) Topping one male gains the superior position and comes down across the anterior portion of the other male and pushes him to the ground in a quick movement, and 3) Continuous contact of the posterior portion of the body. One notable difference was observed. The exaggerated posture of bending over backwards not seen in Sistrurus miliarius was observed on several occasions during this encounter. The apparent winner of the bout was the larger previously unknown male.

22736: The use of automated acoustic receiver arrays has become a popular method for studying the longer-term movements of marine fishes; however, quantifying the effective detection range of these arrays poses challenges and may be important for interpretation of fish movements. We are currently using one such array to monitor the movements of round stingrays in the nearshore waters off Seal Beach, California. The environmental conditions in this area (i.e. shallow water and wave exposure) can greatly attenuate acoustic transmissions and negatively affect the performance of this receiver array. To quantify the detection abilities of this array, we towed a transmitter (pulsing randomly every 60 to 180 sec) throughout the array during high and low tides to simulate fish movements. Over varying tidal heights, 68 ± 9 % (MEAN ± SD) of transmitter pulses were detected within 275 ± 86 m of all automated receivers. An estimated activity space based on receiver detections was 78 % of the size of the activity space determined based on the actual positions of the transmitter taken during simulated tracks. In addition, each receiver had a different effective detection range depending on its specific depth. Because round stingrays show relatively slow and aperiodic movements at Seal Beach, the shallow and wave exposed nature of this area does not appear to significantly influence the detection of tagged stingrays and provides adequate coverage needed to ascertain the longer-term movement patterns of rays at Seal Beach.

22737: In Calakmul, one of the most important Mexican Biosphere Reserves in southeast Mexico, the ichthyofauna is little known. Because of that, we sampled during eighteen months in 64 aquatic systems. A total of 11,658 individuals with 34.5 kg by weight were collected using different fish gears depending on geomorphologic characteristics (beach seine, drop net, hook and line), including photography material as a taxonomic tool in fish determinations. Six families with 19 genera and 31 species cover most of the collected material with Cichlidae family being the most representative with the highest genera (6) and species (13) followed by Poeciliidae (7 genera, 11 species). Considering the numerical abundance, weight and frequency in all sampling stations, Astyanas aeneus, Poecilia mexicana, Gambusia sexradiata, Thorichthys meeki, Rhamdia guatemalensis and Archocentrus octofasciatus were considered dominants. This study is considered an important contribution to the freshwater ichthyofauna of southern Mexico and Central American.

22738: We studied Florida box turtles (Terrapene carolina bauri) in a Pine Rockland forest at the southernmost limit of its range in the lower Florida Keys. Studies have been conducted in the northern parts of its range, but not in southern Florida despite the fact that life history parameters vary latitudinally. The climate in south Florida is sub-tropical and the strong rainfall-driven seasonality in this area resembles that of the tropics and therefore offers a unique opportunity to expand our knowledge of this wide-ranging species. Twelve turtles were monitored with radio telemetry techniques to determine seasonal habitat use and activity patterns on Big Pine Key, FL. Data collected from April 2003 through March 2004 indicate that the rainfall-driven seasonality in sub-tropical Florida has an effect on activity patterns and habitat use. With box turtle populations declining and crucial habitat being destroyed, it is imperative to ascertain the status and habitat requirements of this species in southern Florida.

22739: Of the 16 species of native Eleutherodactylus frogs of Puerto Rico, 12 are threatened or endangered. Three of these endangered species have been declared extinct. Although there have been many studies with this genus in the island, most studies are limited to the common coquí, Eleutherodactylus coqui. There is a great need to assess the status of the other species, particularly with recent reports of populations that have disappeared during the last three decades. Acoustical surveys have been used to search and monitor amphibian populations. One technique used is an automated recorder that records without intervention in a cassette during a desired period of time. I developed an automated recorder that uses a digital recorder instead of the cassette recorder to search for extant populations and to determine the temporal calling patterns of Eleutherodactylus frogs in Puerto Rico. Although there was one paper that describes the calling pattern during the night for fifteen species, the data were recorded systematically for just five species, there were no data about environmental or seasonal variability, and there are conflicting reports about the patterns for several species. Without this information, it is harder for herpetologists and government officials to search for the endangered or threatened species at an optimal period, with higher rates of success in finding an existing population. I have surveyed populations of all extant species in the island to determine their temporal calling patterns and its variation with season, temperature, humidity and precipitation using the automated digital recorders. I have also placed the recorders at historical sites for several species to determine if the declared extinct status of the species or populations is due to the real extinction or the researcher not being there at the appropriate time.

22740: I review studies conducted during the past 15 years on ecology and natural history of Amazonian lizards with comments on some of the species in other habitats (Caatinga, Cerrado, Amazon savanna). The Amazonian lizard fauna varies from locality to locality, but some species have broad distributions. Ecological traits of widespread species are consistent regardless of where they occur, suggesting that the local lizard assemblage may have had little effect on pre-existing ecological traits of some species. Moreover, major clades are ecologically distinct from each other, suggesting a strong historical contribution to present day community structure deeply rooted in the evolutionary history of lizard clades. For example, nearly all Amazonian gymnophthalmids are small in body size and live in leaf litter or on stream edges whereas all Amazonian tropidurids live on open surfaces (rocks, tree trunks, large limbs). Some of the most obvious ecological traits of Amazonian lizards (e.g., ant-eating in tropidurids) can be traced to ancestors living in different environments. I conclude that research on diverse lizard assemblages must consider the impact of long and often independent evolutionary histories of lizard clades in searching for explanations of structure of present day lizard assemblages.

22741: Faunal homogenization occurs when regionally diverse assemblages are replaced with a lower number of tolerant, typically invasive species. Changes in the ratio of highland endemic species to cosmopolitan generalist species can serve as a metric of homogenization among stream fishes. Such evidence has been found in conjunction with increasing development in the Piedmont and Blue Ridge physiographic provinces. Habitat alteration, particularly habitat homogenization, is often a catalyst for faunal homogenization, followed by the introduction of nonnative species concurrent with the extirpation of native species. Altered sediment and hydrologic regimes are likely proximate causes that precipitate habitat and biotic homogenization. However, hypotheses exploring the actual causes of homogenization have not been tested. As the channel morphology of a stream is altered so too are instream habitat units such as riffles, glides, and pools. With infilling by fine sediments, individual habitat types become less distinct and once-heterogeneous reaches are homogenized. With increasing land use intensity, endemic and habitat-specialist fishes are replaced by more cosmopolitan generalist species that are usually found in more lowland areas. Our work focuses on the presumed role that alteration and elimination of specific instream habitat types play in promoting the homogenization of freshwater fish assemblages. Preliminary results strongly point to linkages among deforestation, sediment transport, habitat homogenization, and alterations in the ratio between endemic and cosmopolitan fish species.

22742: Turtles inhabit a wide range of environments, from open ocean, to freshwater ponds, to stark desert. It is this variety of lifestyles that make turtles an interesting group of organisms in which to study olfaction. Olfaction is the detection of air or water born chemicals through the bonding of these chemicals to either olfactory or vomeronasal receptors found in the nose of the organism. Olfactory receptors are thought to bind to general odors and there may be special types for air vs. water bourn odors. Vomeronasal receptors are thought to be primarily responsible for pheromone detection but have been found to bind to general odors in some reptiles (including turtles). A molecular approach to studying olfaction may give clues as to which mechanism of olfaction a turtle is using as well as the importance of olfaction to turtles from different environments. DNA was isolated from the blood of three sea turtles (green, loggerhead, and leatherback), two freshwater turtles (musk and painted), and two terrestrial turtles (box and gopher tortoise). Primers based on conserved regions of olfactory receptor genes in birds and mammals were used to amplify OR genes which were then cloned and sequenced. Sequences with internal stop codons were found in all species of turtle and these genes were assumed nonfunctional. The percentage of OR genes with internal stop codons was higher for aquatic turtles then for land turtles suggesting a lesser degree of OR importance in aquatic turtles. To assess the importance of OR genes in sea turtles, allelic variation was compared in five OR genes across several populations of sea turtles. A high degree of allelic variation would indicate a lesser degree of gene importance to the life history of the animal. Very little allelic variation was found implying a high degree of importance for the genes studied. Aquatic turtles may have fewer functional OR genes but those they do have seem to have selective importance. Research on vomeronasal receptors as well as brain anatomy as related to the olfactory system is being conducted to support these findings. Funding (RGV), NMFS, Honolulu.

22743: The human population of Florida is increasing at a rate of 2.5 million people per decade, which puts increasing demand on natural areas for recreational opportunities. 22744: Green salamanders (Aneides aeneus) are thought to be rock outcrop dwellers, only occasionally using arboreal habitat. 22745: Manipulations of water levels in wetlands are commonly practiced by land managers, but their effects on reptiles and amphibians are studied only rarely. 22746: Elongate body forms have evolved a number of times within vertebrates. There are two mechanisms by which the axial skeleton could become elongated. There could be an increase in total number of vertebrae or an increase in the relative length of the vertebral centrum (aspect ratio). These increases could occur in a specific region of the vertebral column or across the entirety of the axial skeleton. The goal of this study was to determine how elongation occurred in seven groups of actinopterygian fishes (Polypteriformes, Osteoglossomorpha, Elopomorpha, Ostariophysi, Paracanthopterygii, Beloniformes, and Scombroidei). I collected vertebral counts and aspect ratios (centrum length/width) from both the abdominal and caudal vertebral regions for each species examined. Results indicate that elongation generally occurs by an increase in total number of vertebrae and the increases in vertebral number were found to be region specific. I found that increases in number of vertebrae generally occurred in the caudal region with little increase in the number of abdominal vertebrae, but at least one group showed an increase in the number of abdominal vertebrae without an increase in the number of caudal vertebrae. Few lineages were found to have increases in both regions. I also found that increased aspect ratio (centrum elongation) was a factor in axial elongation in at least one group. The increase in aspect ratio was found to be similar in the abdominal and caudal regions. Based on these results, I hypothesize that natural selection on body axis length acts on three independent characters: number of abdominal vertebrae, number of caudal vertebrae, and aspect ratio of all vertebrae. I further hypothesize that separate developmental modules control the number of somites in each region, whereas one developmental module controls vertebral aspect ratio across the entirety of the axial skeleton.

22747: Variability in microsatellite loci was examined in 1262 spotted seatrout in an effort to understand spatial and temporal genetic population structuring in the northern Gulf of Mexico. 22748: Red-eyed treefrogs, Agalychnis callidryas, lay gelatinous egg clutches on vegetation overhanging water, where they are preyed on by egg-eating snakes. As early as 30% before the peak of spontaneous hatching, embryos hatch rapidly in response to snake attack, escaping into the water below. Escape hatching is cued by the physical disturbance of the egg clutch, and can be induced by mechanical playbacks of recorded snake attacks. Nonetheless, other intense but benign disturbances such as rain do not induce early hatching, either live or in playbacks. Thus embryos clearly distinguish among vibration patterns. We used synthetic playback stimuli to map the response of A. callidryas embryos to three simple characteristics of vibrational patterns: the duration of disturbance events, their spacing, and the vibration frequency. Across the range of stimuli tested, there was a single peak of hatching at intermediate values of each parameter, with substantially lower hatching at other values. Furthermore, only stimuli within a fairly narrow range of values for all three parameters elicited substantive hatching; altering even one parameter substantially reduced embryo response. This clearly shows that embryos use multiple features of vibrations concurrently to assess risk. It also suggests that embryos specifically identify certain disturbance patterns as dangerous, rather than hatching in response to disturbance in general save for certain patterns that are perceived as safe. Nonetheless, the synthetic stimuli that elicited the most hatching were not well matched to the most dangerous natural disturbances, snake attacks. This indicates that either embryos measure the key parameters differently than we did, or that our synthetic stimuli do not capture all the information that embryos use to make their hatching decisions.
