22927: The genus Parauchenipterus is a paraphyletic assemblage of 25 nominal species distributed from southern Panama to Argentina. The genus status has changed several times through history, and the specific composition is uncertain. To date, no formal revision of the genus was performed, and confusion surrounds specific names and their usage. Thus the objectives are: the study of relationships of Parauchenipterus species with other auchenipterid taxa, and a taxonomic revision of its members. Based on osteological, sexual dimorphic and gonadal characters three monophyletic groups within Parauchenipterus species are recognized. (1) The Parauchenipterus galeatus group comprises species characterized by a long cleithral process, more than two pairs of gonadal storage lobes and males usually not showing secondary sexual dimorphism. (2) The Parauchenipterus striatulus group is characterized by a short cleithral process, only one pair of gonadal storage pouches and males usually showing secondary sexual dimorphic characters relative to maxillary barbel and dorsal fin spine. These two groups share a unique feature, represented by a pair of tubular caeca anteriorly directed, indicating that they could be sister taxa. (3) The Parauchenipterus insignis group, which has been recently studied, and will be removed to a new genus. Although several characteristics distinguish this group from other Parauchenipterus species, only the following synapomorphies are listed: (1) swim gas bladder with two large caeca posteriorly directed; (2) maxillary barbel with a fully ossified core; (3) large dermal papillae on dorsal cranial surface and inner margin of the maxillary barbel. The Parauchenipterus insignis group comprises all the species north and westward Lake Maracaibo drainage, and one species from the River Uruguay drainage. Despite this disjunct distribution the River Uruguay species, Parauchenipterus teaguei, shares all the synapomorphic features of the group with slightly modifications and some autapomorphic features. Therefore it is provisionally included among its northern congeners.

22928: Over the last decade a premium has been placed on priority-setting because the rapidly growing list of species threatened with extinction has overwhelmed limited conservation resources. The ‘biodiversity hotspots’ concept, formalized in 2000, maximizes return on conservation investment by focusing on the top twenty-five most imperiled regions of exceptional vascular plant and tetrapod vertebrate endemism. Because of its clarity, the hotspots strategy has been at the center of major funding initiatives by private and public organizations, including the largest private conservation donation to date. Of the world’s 300 living tortoise and freshwater turtle species, roughly 50% were considered threatened by the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) in 2000. This emerging global turtle survival crisis has created an immediate need to identify priorities for turtle conservation. Toward this end, an examination of species’ geographic distributions reveals some important trends. Nearly half of all living species are found in just six priority areas comprising less than 1% of the land surface of the earth. More than 80% of living species are found in 21 of the 25 hotspots, three of which correspond to priority areas. Just one hotspot in Asia contains roughly 20% of the world’s living species, 50% of which are endangered. Therefore, directing conservation resources toward hotspots will most efficiently benefit the greatest number and many of the most imperiled tortoise and freshwater turtle species

22929: Species of Gymnotus are substantially more diverse than has previously been recognized. From examination of 775 museum lots bearing 2721 specimens from 27 museum collections we recognize 32 valid species of Gymnotus, the majority of which (18/32) occur in the Amazon basin. We compiled a data matrix of 113 phenotypic characters of color pattern, squamation, morphometrics, meristics, laterosensory system, osteology, myology, electric organ morphology, and electric organ discharge parameters. These characters were coded for 41 OTUs including all 32 recognized Gymnotus species and 6 allopatric populations of the widespread species G. carapo. Analysis using maximum parsimony yielded 8 equally parsimonious trees (each of l=387, ci=0.37, rc=0.26) the strict consensus of which is presented as a working hypothesis of Gymnotus interrelationships. The resulting topology is used to recognize three species-groups; 1, group A with two species restricted to Middle America, without oblique pigment bands; 2, group B with 13 species in South America east of the Andes, most with unpaired bands and straight band- margins; and 3, group C with 16 species (including the type of the genus G. carapo) found throughout cis- and trans-Andean tropical South America, most with paired bands and wavy band-margins. Species in group C are readily recognized by a clear patch at the caudal end of the anal fin and two pores at the dorso-posterior corner of the preopercle. The basal node is between clades endemic to Middle and South America. Within group C there are at least three trans- Andean sister-taxon pairs, suggesting a minimum date for the origin of this species group in the Miocene. Preliminary results from analysis of mitochondrial cytochrome b and nuclear RAG2 genes (total about 2355 bp) are consistent with the division of Gymnotus into these species groups. The phylogenetic patterns recovered suggest that evolution in Gymnotus is a continental, not basin-wide, phenomenon; i.e., Amazonian species richness is not a consequence of strictly Amazonian processes. These patterns are similar to those of other highly diverse groups of Neotropical fishes, and do not resemble those of monophyletic, rapidly generated species flocks (e.g., African great lake cichlids).

22930: The construction of series of dams transforms rivers into chains of artificial lakes. Impoundment unavoidably results in changes in species composition and abundance. A new trophic structure is expected to develop as a consequence of alterations in resource availability and the capability of species to exploit them. The Serra da Mesa Hydroelectric Dam (SM) impounded the upper Tocantins River in 1996 and began operating in 1998. The area studied had been subject to several disturbances, such as construction of SM detour tunnels and dam, and release of anoxic turbine water. In Jan/2002 a second dam (SD) was installed downstream. In this case study we present data on the trophic ecology of the fish community in this stretch of the river before (2001) and after (2002) the installation of SD. The feeding habits of species were identified through stomach content analyses, grouping them in six trophic guilds. After SD, captures increased, but relative importance of guilds changed. Biomass contribution of detritivores and invertivores decreased, whereas omnivores, represented mainly by geophagine cichlids, remained constant, as did the diets of these species. The importance of piscivores doubled, mainly from the invasion of large schools of immature Boulengerella cuvieri and non-reproductive adult Galeocharax cf. gulo five months after the beginning of reservoir formation. The former became established and grew, whereas the latter disappeared. The most remarkable feature was the increase of fish as food resource, which also occurred in the SM Reservoir, but in lower magnitude. Downstream, the main prey was Anchoviella sp., a pelagic zooplanktivore consumed also by non-piscivores. Some of these consequences of reservoir formation are well documented; however, it is important to understand how far they represent a general pattern or can be attributed to the role of historical and local conditions

22931: This work has sought to characterize the possibility of rearing and breeding turtles in captivity as a way to guarantee new alternatives of sustainable use rather than the present techniques of active exploitation of natural resources. 22932: We studied habitat fragmentation and gene flow in a population of the redback salamanders (Plethodon cinereus) in Virginia, USA. Specifically, we looked at a population of salamanders living in a forest bisected by a four-lane highway. We asked whether subpopulations on opposite sides of the road showed higher levels of genetic differentiation than subpopulations on the same side of the road. We developed primers for six microsatellite loci; heterozygosity ranged from 30% to 70%. Hierarchical analysis showed evidence for small, but statistically significant differentiation due to the highway. Studies of additional road sites will help us determine the generality of these effects and whether roads of different size and age reduce gene flow among terrestrial salamander populations.

22933: The mating season in the northern watersnake (Nerodia sipedon) occurs in the spring concomitant with vitellogenesis. Mating occurs primarily in trees and bushes which overhang the water. Watersnakes access these basking/mating sites from the water, thus, the terrestrial trailing of a female, typical of most of the snakes studied, cannot occur. Field observations indicate that males systematically search for females from the water. We suggest that watersnake pheromones are heavy, volatile compounds that accumulate along the surface of the water and that males climb branches that are in the vicinity of pheromone concentrations. In field experiments, males are able to locate caged (hidden) attractive females that were placed in trees, over the water or on the shore next to water, without use of trails. On any given day, with appropriate temperatures, the majority of females are not attractive, indicating the females do not produce the attractant continuously during vitellogenesis. Our data suggest that less than 10 percent of the reproductive females are attractive on any one day. In addition to pheromones, males use other cues to locate females including systematic searching of bushes and movement towards moving snakes. Courtship may last from minutes to over one hour and most courtships occurring late in the mating season do not result in mating.

22934: The family Samaridae has 28 nominal species or subspecies, 22 of which are recognized in this study. New species are described, two species and one subspecies are synonymized and two species names are resurrected. An artificial key was constructed for all species. The family is shown to be monophyletic, as are the three genera comprising the family; Plagiopsetta being the most plesiomorphic. Samaris and Samariscus are sister groups. Numerous apomorphies corroborate the monophyly of the S. cristatus complex (Samaris cristatus, S. cacatuae, S. ornatus and S. sp). In Samariscus, S. nielseni, S. corallinus and S. triocellatus form a monophyletic group. The family is restricted to the Indo-West Pacific. Species numbers are highest in the Indo- Malaysian region, drop off with increasing distance and are not found in the extreme eastern Pacific due to the eastern Pacific barrier.

22935: The Wilbur-Collins (W-C) model is based on the idea that the developmental rates of amphibians are moderated by their growth rates, and that for each species there is a minimum and a maximum size at metamorphosis. Between these sizes, an animal that is growing faster than a target rate will remain in the aquatic environment for further growth, while one that is growing more slowly will initiate metamorphosis. The W-C model has been used to predict how the metamorphic parameters of individuals and the distributions of age and size at metamorphosis in populations respond to environments of different quality and variability. Most studies have found that individuals respond as predicted by the W-C model, at least early in their larval periods. The results at the population level are less clear; some studies have found responses consistent with their W-C predictions, others have not. These differences could be caused by some species not following the W-C model, or by oversimplification of its predictions. I used simulations of tadpole growth and development to examine how distributions of age and size at metamorphosis should respond to environmental conditions, and found that almost any pattern can be produced by populations of individuals following the W-C model. I also examined size and age distributions for many populations with known histories, and found that although the pattern of growth and development of individuals of many species is approximated by the W-C model, the relative importance of size-maximization and time-minimization, and thus the likely true form of models for metamorphic decision making, appear to differ among species.

22936: The amphibian chytrid fungus, Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, is probably responsible for mass dieoffs of some amphibian populations. It also occurs in populations of many species that have not suffered mass dieoffs. In many of these species, it is often found in 5% or less of individuals examined in the field. However, in some of these species, it easily infects and kills 100% of exposed animals in laboratory experiments. Data on the growth and survival of the chytrid fungus both in vitro and in vivo indicate that standard environmental conditions for maintaining amphibians in the laboratory are also near optimal for the chytrid fungus, and therefore for the progress of chytridiomycosis. Maintaining animals in the laboratory under a wider range of environmental conditions affects the progress of the disease, and can even cure it. In the field, amphibians encounter a much wider range of thermal and hydric conditions than they do under standard laboratory conditions. At least some of the species that are less vulnerable to chytridiomycosis spend substantial fractions of their time in habitats that are unfavorable to its growth and development. We suggest that many differences in vulnerability among species and between laboratory and field populations are due to differences in behavior and habitat selection; understanding how these vary among species and across time is likely to provide insight into the spatial and temporal patterns of dieoffs caused by chytridiomycosis.

22937: Sexual differentiation in reptiles with temperature-dependent sex determination (TSD) is known to be influenced by several factors including nest site choice and maternally derived hormones. Collectively these influences may play an adaptive role for the maintenance of TSD. In wide ranging species, these influences may be important for adjusting the dynamics of TSD to better match local environmental conditions. With a range from Massachusetts to Texas, the diamondback terrapin, Malaclemys terrapin, is a wide ranging emydid turtle that shows geographic variation in reproductive strategy. Northern populations exhibit a shorter nesting season and deposit fewer clutches characterized by a larger number of smaller eggs. More southern populations have a longer nesting season where more clutches of larger, but fewer, eggs are laid. To analyze the potential variation in developmental characters associated with TSD, eggs were collected from three terrapin populations and incubated at 29.5° C. The southernmost population examined produced more male hatchlings whereas the two more northern populations produced clutches with a female sex bias. Female gonads one month after hatching had higher aromatase activity than males, but brain tissues showed no sexual aromatase differences. Furthermore, hatchling lipid analysis indicated a higher proportion of non-polar lipids in the southern population than in both northern populations. The data show strong support for geographic variation in TSD dynamics in wide ranging populations.

22938: The potamotrygonid stingrays are the only elasmobranchs completely adapted for living in freshwater environments and are restricted to some Neotropical river basins. Dorsal color patterns have been widely used as important criteria in the identification of freshwater stingrays. The intraespecific dorsal color variability (polychromatism) that occurs in the Potamotrygonidae Family almost always results in misidentifications or the use of different designations for a same species. A total of 385 specimens was capture in the Marajó Bay region during the years of 2000, 2001 and 2002. All of them were previously identified as Potamotrygon scobina. These specimens were separated into two size groups that included 80 neonates / juveniles and 305 sub adults / adults. A dorsal color pattern characterization study was carried out considering the shape, distribution and presence / absence of previously defined figures. Three dorsal color patterns were observed for neonate / juveniles individuals and four patterns were verified for sub adults / adults specimens. The sub adults and adults specimens had 31 external morphometric measurements taken that were submitted to multivariated statistical analysis. Principal Component and Discriminant Function Analysis were used to verify the existence of differentiated groups. The results obtained indicated that all four color patterns overlap and that no particular group was formed. Results also indicated that the P. scobina specimens sampled formed a single group independent of the variations among the dorsal color patterns. Conclusively, two new color patterns were described for neonate / juvenile specimens and three new patterns were included for sub adult / adults. Extreme care is recommended when using uniquely dorsal color patterns to identify potamotrygonid freshwater stingrays.

22939: The present study objective is to relate the presence of loricariid catfishes to microhabitat by using standardized sample effort. A total of nine sites were sampled during seven surveys. Sites were located in different reaches of a coastal stream (Pereque-Acu river, Paraty county, Rio de Janeiro state), in altitudes that ranged from 910 m to 5 m above sea level. Catch effort was previously divided into gear/microhabitat match categories. Microhabitats were defined by its substrate and its current intensity. Six substrates (with and without water current) were found in the basin, totalizing twelve microhabitats. Sieves, hand-nets and kicking-nets were used for the fish sampling. Underwater observations provided additional data. Seven species were registered, totalizing 1026 specimens: Schizolecis guntheri, Hisonotus notatus, Neoplecostomus sp., Hemipsilichthys spn, Loricariidae sp.5, Pareiorhina rudolphi and Kronichthys heylandi. Pareiorhina rudolphi and Loricariidae sp.5 were caught mostly in headwater reaches, occupying different habitats. Loricariidae sp.5 was caught mostly in rocky substrates without current (pools), while Pareiorhina rudolphi was collected in riffle habitat, with sandy or rocky substrate. The species found strictly on the upper reaches (Neoplecostomus sp., Hemipsilichthys spn) were caught exclusively in rocky surfaces with current. The other three species were caught mostly in medium and lower reaches. Schizolecis guntheri was present in 7 different microhabitats, with no distinct preference. Hisonotus notatus was collected mostly in riparian vegetation with water current, but was also present in steep banks without current and sandy substrate with water current. Kronichthys heylandi was most abundant in riparian vegetation and rocky substrate, both with water current.

22940: The genus Hemipsilichthys Eigenmann & Eigenmann (Loricariidae: Siluriformes) is composed of small to medium-sized species of armored catfishes. Eighteen species are recognized belonging to genus, most of them from the southern and southeastern regions of Brazil. The present study objective is to describe a new species of Hemipsilichthys. The description was made based on external morphology of 14 specimens (22mm to 85mm Standard Lenght) caught in the upper reaches of the Pereque-Acu river, a coastal stream in Paraty county, Rio de Janeiro state. This species can be distinguished from all other Hemipsilichthys fishes by having the dorsal count one spine and eight soft rays (instead of one and seven) and by presenting very small hypertrophied cheek's odontodes. 22941: The genus Eigenmannia comprehends a number of cryptic species, many of them still non- described, most of which present different chromosome number and formulae and variable systems of morphologically differentiated sex chromosomes. 22942: The family Loricariidae has a great number of species (ca. 700); however, only about 90 were analyzed cytogenetically. With the objective to identify the trends of chromosomic evolution in this family, the available cytogenetic information as well as original data obtained in the present study were analyzed. Loricariidae has been divided in six subfamilies, being Lithogeninae the most primitive. However, for this subfamily no cytogenetic data are available. Species of the subfamily Neoplecostominae, considered the most primitive after Lithogeninae, presented 2n=54 chromosomes with simple interstitial nucleolus organizer regions (NORs). Most species of Hypoptopomatinae also presented 2n=54 and simple interstitial NORs. The largest karyotypic variation was observed among Hypostominae, with diploid number ranging from 2n=52 in Liposarcus anisitsi to 2n=96 in Upsilodus sp.; NORs are single or multiples. In Ancistrinae diploid numbers ranged from 2n=38 to 2n=54 in two undescribed Ancistrus species and the NORs were single. In Loricariinae the diploid numbers ranged from 2n=36 in Rineloricaria latirostris to 2n=74 in Sturisoma nigrirostrum and the NORs were single. All subfamilies of Loricariidae presented species with NORs in interstitial position, and this type is also found even in some species in those subfamilies where the terminal NORs is the most frequent. Considering the distribution of the diploid numbers and the number and position of NORs in the species it can be supposed that the 2n=54 and interstitial NORs can be considered as a primitive karyotypic characteristics for Loricariidae. In Ancistrinae, an apparent decrease of the diploid number seems to be occurred, while in Hypostominae an evident increase of this diploid number occurred. Among Loricariinae some species present an increase and other a decrease in diploid numbers. It is suggested that chromosome changes played an important role in species diversification in Loricariidae and each group evolved independently concerning the modification of their karyotypes.

22943: Rio das Velhas, the most important tributary of the São Francisco river, is one of the few South American rivers that were intensively studied in the 19th century. Information on the material collected by J.T. Reinhardt and described in 1875 in a monograph by C.F. Lutken (Velhas- Flodens Fiske) is now available in a Portuguese-language version. The prospect of recovery of the fish fauna in Rio das Velhas is evaluated with basis on data collected in the past, recent fish collections in the main stem, tributaries and Lagoa Santa Central Lake, and the current uses of this river basin. One hundred and seven species were recorded from 1998 to 2002. Of these, 93 were identified in the main stem, 81 in the tributaries and only ten in the Lagoa Santa Central Lake. The most significant source of impact to the river biota is non-treated sewage from the Belo Horizonte Metropolitan Region, which has a population of 4.5 million. The richness and diversity of species reach their lowest levels immediately downstream of the point where sewage from Belo Horizonte is discharged into Rio das Velhas. Other detected impacts are mining activities in headwater areas, removal of riparian vegetation, water diversion, and the introduction of alien species, the latter being a major cause of extinction of approximately 70% of the native fauna in the Lagoa Santa Central Lake. Three main factors improve the chances of recovery or minimization of these impacts: (1) new sewage treatment facilities now being implemented in Belo Horizonte and other cities within the basin, (2) the still preserved connectivity with the São Francisco river system, with no natural or artificial obstacles; and (3) the existence of environmentally healthy tributaries, such as the Cipó river, supporting approximately 75% of all species identified in the Rio das Velhas basin.

22944: An investigation carried out during the year of 2000 on the reproduction of fish species captured in Araguaia River, near Cantão State Park of Tocantins, showed that from the total of 137 species present in the area, 59 (43%) were spawning. Reproductive intensity (RI) was measured by the proportional number of females with ripe ovaries of a certain species. The results showed that reproduction occurred with different intensity at the several sampling sites suggesting that spawning takes place more intensively at sites that are influenced only by Araguaia River (Ariranha, Narú and Perdidos Lakes), as opposed to those that are influenced by Côco River (Casé Lake) and Javaezinho River (Volta Grande Lake). Considering the different hydrological periods (flood, lowing, low and rising) it was observed a clear variation of RI with increased spawning activity during the rising through flood periods. Although the role of environmental parameters is little known, there are evidences that changes in the water level is the key factor to neotropical freshwater fish reproductive processes; the rising of the water would trigger the process whereas the peak of flood would finalize it. The overall RI determined for the fishfauna of Cantão (1,12) is low when compared to other similar places within the Amazonia (Catalão Lake =1,56 and Inácio Lake =1,26, both near Manaus) and outside (Paraná Basin - 1,40), suggesting the area is mainly used as feeding and possibly nursery grounds rather than spawning. It is important to note, however, that 22% of the species that reproduce in the area are of commercial value, therefore, preservation of the system like it is today is not only essential to guarantee the diversity and the biological integrity of the ictiofauna but also to maintain the level of production of the stocks.
22945: Acoustic communication is restricted under noisy conditions. Heterospecific sounds may reduce signal-to-noise ratios for vocalizing anurans. Thus, the need of communication may constrain the assemblage of species-rich communities of tropical frogs. Each frog species uses a frequency range (i.e., spectral window) and, thus, established co-occurring species with overlapping spectral windows should diverge evolutionarily in the frequency domain of their calls or in their temporal call patterns. Calling phenology may reflect restrictions imposed by reproductive modes, rather than temporal partitioning among spectrally overlapping frogs. Additionally, spectral divergence is constrained by the size of sound-producing structures, pleiotropically linked to body size, and by the auditory sensitivity. Although variation in spectral sensitivity may be as important as call variation for spectral partitioning in frog communities, it has been rarely studied at the behavioral level. We used the phonotactic approach of territorial E. femoralis males to test (1) whether spectral sensitivity fits the distribution of the call frequency at the population level, and (2) whether spectral sensitivity has the evolutionary potential to vary within a single species and among communities of frogs. We manipulated the frequency range of synthetic advertisement calls and performed playback experiments in the field. From binary data we derived spectral sensitivity curves, as well as width estimates of sensitivity windows. Male spectral sensitivity was wider and slightly asymmetric in comparison to the call-frequency distribution at the population level. Males responded even to calls with frequency ranges beyond the population and species limits. At first sight, the wide spectral sensitivity of E. femoralis does not strongly support the prediction of differential use of spectral windows. However, the results from four populations indicate that the amplitude of spectral sensitivity windows is narrower where calling males have a higher chance of channel interference.

22946: The feeding biology of some snakes is characterized by occasional ingestion of large meals interspaced by prolonged periods of fasting. This particular feeding biology is associated with several specializations related to prey capture, ingestion, and digestion. Food acquisition and processing causes a number of physiological responses, which cause metabolism to be elevated. Such metabolic increment is affected by proximal factors (e.g., meal mass, temperature, etc.) and has further consequences on the energetic for feeding. Herein, we discuss the proximal factors affecting the metabolism of rattlesnake, Crotalus durissus terrificus, and boa, Boa constrictor, during predation and digestion. In both species, aerobic metabolism is significantly elevated during prey capture and ingestion and this increase is affected by relative prey size. During predation, boa experience higher metabolic rates than rattlesnake particularly due to the cost of prey constriction. The relative cost of prey capture is inversely correlated with prey size in boa, but not in rattlesnake. For both species, it seems that predation is not completely sustained by aerobic metabolism, and participation of anaerobic pathway is likely to occur. Digestion is accompanied by significant increase of aerobic metabolism, which peaks within 24 – 48 h after feeding and return to fasting values within 8 – 15 days post-feeding. Maximum rates of metabolism during digestion may attain values up to 8 times above that measured during rest in fasting snakes. Such increase in metabolism may exceed the maximum rates attained during forced exercise. Metabolism during digestion is affected by prey size and temperature in both species. In general, higher temperatures result in greater increases of post-prandial metabolism accompanied by shorter digestion duration. Post-prandial metabolism and digestion duration increase with meal size, while energetic profit is not altered. In rattlesnakes, it seems that prey envenomation and the occurrence of a post-prandial thermofilic response facilitates digestion. Financial support by Fapesp, CNPq and FUNDUNESP.

22947: Itapiraco forest reserve is one of the last fragments of forest on Sao Luis island, Maranhao, northeastern Brazil. This fragment has been severely effected by human activity. We made a herpetological survey in this area, which harbours species from the Amazon region and the Cerrado. We sampled six habitats: gallery forest (GF), mesophylous forest (MF), secondary forest in the first stage of regeneration (SFI) and in a more advanced stage (SFII), clearings (CL) and open areas (OA). In each area 3 sets of pit-fall traps were laid totaling 18. The sets consisted of 25 2-liter bottles without necks positioned in 5 lines of 5 bottles. 50 cm was the distance between the bottles. Beside the traps another hole was dug, 1 m in depth and diameter. 576 hours of visual observations in quadrats of 5m x 5m at randomly selected sites within each habitat complemented the findings. These observations were made in the form of weekly visits from August/1999- September/2000. We found anurans from 5 families, 12 genera and 21 species, lizards from 8 families, 17 genera and 18 species and snakes from 5 families, 16 genera and 19 species. We also found 2 species of amphisbaenids, one of Kinosternidae and one caiman. SFII and OA had the greatest richness of species, 26 and 21 respectively. SFI had the least richness, 16. For snakes and anurans the similarity of habitat was low, but for lizards/amphisbaenids it was high (Cj = 0.7 between SFII and MF). The high equitability (J' > 0.91), considering the quantitative data, influenced the high values of diversity in CL (H' = 1.57) for anurans, in SFI (H' = 2.22) for lizards/amphisbaenids, and in OA (H' = 1.67) for snakes. The majority of anurans (7 out of 10 spp) and lepidosaurians (22 out of 30 spp) showed a narrow spatial niche, which indicates habitat specialists. However, 14 of these species were rare in the area. If the human impact doesn't stop only the few generalists and open area species will account for the herpetological diversity of this endangered reserve.

22949: Consuming chelonian products is a tradition in Amazonia, even though the sale is illegal. We, bimonthly, monitored from 1997 the 2000, 13 of the 69 commercial registered turtle farms in Amazonas (64.98 % in Manaus, Manacapuru and Iranduba) and observed that 50% of the 35 properties possess of 9 to 35 ha; 50% of the dams are of 1-2 ha and 60% of nurseries have of 30- 500 m2; 60% possess between 1000 and 5000 animals, representing a small economic return, since that 30% possess more than 10,000 turtles. In 60%, the density in the nursery is of 0.5 to 5 animals/m2. Food varies, 40% receive visceras and/or ration, 20% fish and 20% vegetables. In the 1° year, hatchlings of P. expansa fed with rations for fish of 30-42% CP reach greater weight (603.96 ± 33.42 g) and daily weight gain (0.769 ± 0.71 g/day) than the ones fed with fish (186.69 ± 74.9 g and 0.304 ± 0.29 g/day) and with vegetables (31.66 ± 1.2 g and 0.121 ± 0.17 g/day). Animals fed with larger amount of animal protein present greater daily weight gain (DWG), average DWG = 0.554 ± 0.13 g/day, than the ones that had received protein vegetal, DWG = 0.375 ± 0.31 g/day. In the 2° year of cultivation, animals fed with visceras bovine has a trend to have greater DWG (1.82 ± 0.97 g/day) than the fed ones with fish (1.31 ± 1.1 g/day), vegetables (1.20 ± 1.27 g/day) and ration (1.06 ± 1.26 g/day). The density is another factor that influences the DWG in the nurseries. We verify a DWG = 0.9 for 78 animals/m2, DWG = 0.4 g/day for 5-60 animals/m2 and DWG = 0.25 g/day for 105 animals/m2. The excellent density of culture in the 1° year is of 65-100 animals/m2 with DWG = 0.68 g/day. The cost with ration is of U$ 1.45 to produce 1 kg of BW and in a super-intensive cultivation in tank-net net income of U$ 246.24/m3 can be gotten.

22950: The canary rockfish (Sebastes pinniger) has been an important part of the recreational and commercial rockfish fisheries from southeast Alaska to southern California, but stocks have declined considerably over the past few decades. This rockfish is thought to be long-lived with an estimated longevity approaching 84 years, based upon detailed analysis of growth zones in otolith sections. For the purpose of monitoring stocks, age composition is routinely estimated by counting growth zones in these otoliths using the break-and-burn technique; however, such age estimates and high longevities for this species have remained unvalidated. Typical age validation techniques have limited application for the canary rockfish because they are deep dwelling and appear to be long-lived fish. In this study, we have taken the unaged otolith of the pair from aged fish and applied one of two radiometric age validation techniques: 1) the disequilibria of lead-210 and radium-226, and 2) the time-specific, bomb-produced radiocarbon marker. By removing core material from otoliths and either analyzing it for lead-210 and radium-226 or bomb radiocarbon we will provide a basis for age validation of the canary rockfish and present a useful corroboration between the two age validation techniques.

22951: Road mortality of snakes is an issue both locally in the southeastern United States and globally. Although only relative impacts can be ascertained due to a lack of data in true abundance of many local populations, it is commonly thought that this mortality is detrimental to wild populations. Consistently finding certain species of snakes dead on the road suggests vulnerability for particular snakes. However, it is unknown whether other species of snakes not found on the road are also impacted by this development. Roads potentially act as a barrier for snakes unwilling to venture out onto the road, therefore, serving as a source of habitat fragmentation for certain species. Information from a Savannah River Site (SRS) long-term database (>35 years) will be presented regarding the perceived abundance of certain species found on the road in relation to species found through off-road measures. These data are compared with current research examining the propensity of different species to avoid or cross the road through a series of behavioral trials that test the responses of snakes to road encounters. Preliminary results, including crossing frequencies, speeds, and angles, in addition to avoidance numbers, are presented for several species of SRS snakes. Correlating information obtained from the behavioral trials and the database will permit the investigation of species-specific road impacts and allow insight into a currently blurry picture of road impacts.

22952: Despite recent and rapid technological advances in science as a whole, the aspect dealing with biodiversity assessments has sadly not shared the same fortune. Our ignorance on the number and nature of species populating the planet stretches far and wide, including amphibians. The number of recognized amphibian species has more than doubled since 1970, and over 5,500 species are currently recognized. However, recent and ongoing research on a number of cryptic genera such as Adenomera, small species of Hyla, Osteocephalus, Phrynopus and Scinax reveal that amphibian species diversity is much higher than what is currently acknowledged. Combining the data from current research on these species complexes and undersampled groups, with trends derived from reports of new species in traditionally species-rich families over the past decade, we generate estimates of amphibian diversity through extrapolation. In the light of declining amphibian populations, comparisons of these estimates, as well as some possible scenarios that could have bearings on conservation decision-making, are discussed.

22953: A subsistence ornamental fishery has existed in the Rio Negro basin since the discovery of the Cardinal Tetra (Paracheirodon axelrodi) in the 1950’s. Rummy-nose tetras, Hemigrammus bleheri and Petitella georgiae, comprise approximately 5% of the total ornamental fish export of the region (>50 million since 2000). This study examined the feeding habits and reproductive biology of H. bleheri. Samples were taken from the igarapé Zamula (00°50′24″ S; 62°45′67″ W), between November 2000 and April 2002. A total of 220 rummy-nose tetras were collected, among them 191 were H. bleheri and 29 P. georgiae. During the period of rising water level, H. bleheri were caught more frequently in the igapó (flooded forest) at a depth to 1.5 m, while in the low water season they were found along the margin of igarapé (forest stream) at a depth to 0.5 m. The water conditions were: pH, 3.0-5.0; dissolved oxigen 1.6-4.7 mg/l; conductivity, 6.6-12.7 µS; temperature 25.3 - 29.2 °C. Stomach content analyses of 133 specimens have shown that H. bleheri is omnivorous. The frequencies of occurrence in the diet include algae (87.0%), Cladoceras (83.0%), animal residue (58.0%), plant debris (41.0%), insect parts (38.0%), eggs (17.0%), seeds (7.0%) and others (5.0%). H. bleheri possesses a relatively short intestine, about 68% of SL and isometric with growth. The sex ratio of H. bleheri showed a slight predominance of females (χ2=2.67). Females also reach a larger size (38 mm SL) than males (33 mm SL). The mean size at the first sexual maturation for male is 24 mm SL, and 26 mm SL for female. Gonad development analyses (n=45) revealed that oocytes varied in diameter from 0.2 to 0.7 mm, with two distinct size modes. The fecundity varied between 179 (30.9 mm SL) to 721 (37.2 mm SL). Histology section of ovary indicated that females mature when water is rising (February-May). A partial discharge of eggs generally occurs in March and a greater or more complete discharge ocurrs in May. (CNPq no. 46.6098/2001-4 & 550367/2001-2)

22954: A taxonomic revision of the genus Gerres in America. Gerres cinereus (Walbaum 1792) is the only nominal species recognized for the genus Gerres in America, however our recent studies based on both morphometric and osteological evidence suggest that actually there are two sibling species of yellow fin mojarra in the tropical and subtropical coastal waters of America: Gerres cinereus in the Atlantic and Gerres simillimus proposed by Regan in 1906-1908 for the Pacific. Our survey was based in two morphometric methods, a classic one and the so called box truss, the fist one was use to compare with published data and the second one for discriminate the shape. Our sample include material from CAS, IBUNAM, UABC, ECOSUR and CICIMAR; for the osteological comparison we disarticulated, clear and stained more than 20 specimens from both sides of America. We show in this poster our statistical and osteological results that support the validity of Gerres simillimus contrary to Meek and Hildebrand (1925) proposal when they synonymized it with Gerres cinereus. A detailed osteological study is currently being conducted by one of us (AAM).

22955: The great diversity of fishes in the mid Rio Negro basin supports a flourishing ornamental fishery. More than 50 million live tropical fishes are exported annually through the town of Barcelos, providing over 60% of the income revenue for the municipality. Bleeding-heart tetras, locally called “Rosacéu”, are a group of heavily exported species. This study is to identify the species included in the rosacéu-group, their habitats and associated ichthyofauna in the floodplain. Seven expeditions were made between October 2000 and April 2002 in the lower reaches of Igarapé Zamula (00° 50′24″ S; 62° 45′67″ W), a tributary of the Rio Negro. This stream is shallow (less than 1.5 m in depth) with a low pH (3.8-5.6) and conductivity (5.0-16.5 µS); moderately high water temperature (25.3-35.5°C) and dissolved O2 (2.26 - 4.77mg/l). Samples were made in two distinct habitats: the margin of the igarapé (forest stream), and the igapó (flooded forest). Fishes were collected with rapiché dip-net, cylindrical and cacur traps. Color pattern, body shape, premaxillary and maxillary bones were used diagnostically to identify five species from this rosacéu-group, which includes Hyphessobrycon copelandi, H. socolofi, H. erythrostigma, Megalamphodus megalopterus and Hemigrammus elegans. The numbers of rosacéus captured varied between the igarapé and igapó habitats. During the lower water period (September – December), the group represented 6.5% of total catch along the margin of the igarapé, and 38.1% in the igapó. In high water season (February – May), the relative abundance was 9.9% in the margin of igarapé, and 29% in the igapó. The rosacéu-group is captured more frequently with Hemigrammus analis, Carnegiella marthae, Curimatopsis evelynae, Moenkhausia colletti and Apistogramma spp. during the low water period (September – December), and with Carnegiella marthae, M. colletti, Microschemobrycon sp., Hemigrammus bellottii, Hemigrammus analis, Nannostomus spp., Crenuchus and Apistogramma spp. during the flood season (February – May). 22957: These paper has as objective to diagnose the fishing, production, composition and fishing effort and characterizing the fisherman (social - economic partner) on the Porto Velho fishing market in the years of 1999 the 2001. The data were obtained from the fishing statistics of the fishing colony and interviews using questionnaires with the fishing and owners of boat. The fishing production in 1999 was 528,970 kg, in 2000 was 438,589kg in 2001 was 782,534 kg. Thirty seven species of fish had arrived at the market, the main species of fish more intensely commercialized had been Curimata (Prochilodus nigricans), Dourada (Brachyplatystoma flavicans), Pacu (Myleus sp.and Mylossoma sp), Sardine (Triportheus sp) and Branquinha (Curimata sp). In Porto Velho there are only 80 fisherman working and only 20 boats. The capture for unit of effort observed was: 9.99 Kg of fishes for liters of diesel used; 175 kg fishy for day fished. The fishing art more used was the net of launches and the malhadeira. The majority of the fisherman lives in the city and dedicated exclusively for fishing. Generally they spend 10 to 20 days in the river or until reaching the capacity of the boat, that in the majority are of small the 6,000 transport varying of 5,000 kg, the average of members for boat was 6 people. The profit acquired is not more them R$300 (US$80) for fishery, the majority of them received the safe unemployment, but is not satisfactory.

22958: This study was carried on in the Amazon River in the vicinity of Leticia. In order to stablish the trophic structure of the fish community we analyzed stomach contents of 44 species captured on the Amazon River in a low water period (August to December, 2000). We concluded that most of the items consumed during this period were autoctonous since all catches were done in the main channel of the river. it seems that detritivory is the base of the trophic chains since the highest value of fish biomas. corresponds to detritivorous fishes, followed by omnivorous, carnivorous and planctivorous. The planctivorous had the minor value of biomas . This work was part of the project “Fishes of the Leticia region” sponsored by the Universidad Nacional de Colombia and CYTED of Spain.

22959: In the most advanced forms of Chondrichthyes the brain/body weight ratio (relative brain weight) matches those found in birds and mammals, and surpass those of other vertebrates. According to the recent studies the largest relative brain weights belong to the species of the Myliobatiformes order, e.g. the Mobula japanica. The determinants of this conspicuous brain size are the telencephalon and cerebellum. Size and outer structure of the cerebellum extremely diverges among Chondrichthyes (Northcutt, 1978), in several groups ( Isurus, Dasyatis, Mobula) the gyrification matches the mammalian and avian cerebella. Intraspecific variations of cerebellar morphology can be considerable, but the investigation in a Dasyatis sp. could not found it to be correlated to size or sex. The neuronal structure of cerebellum is similar in all Chondrichthyes (actually, in all Vertebrates), as we also found in Raja erinacea, Dasyatis americana and pastinaca, and Mobula japanica. Immunostaining against GFAP revealed astrocytes in the molecular layer, similar to birds and mammals, whereas it detected no Bergmann-glia. The size of the cerebellum did not differ significantly between males and females, but in the latter ones a leftward prominence caught the eye, suggesting a sexual dimorphism. Although the female cerebella were recognizable by their asymmetry, even a series of measurements performed on 5-5 male and female cerebella, could not found a parameter to prove the difference significantly. The investigation continues in the analysis of the surface pattern, to reveal its regularities and coin a terminology for its description. In this analysis the gyrification index is to be determined, like in the cortex of mammals (see e.g., Zilles et al., 1988, 1989), and a higher number of specimens are to be investigated.

22960: On a recent collecting trip to the Rupununi of Guyana, a wealth of poorly known or undescribed species of the loricariid subfamily Hypostominae were collected. Collections included two undescribed members of the Hypostomus cochliodon group, an undescribed Hypancistrus related to H. inspector, and a Peckoltia that may represent an undescribed genus. Collections were obtained from the Rupununi/Essequibo and the Takutu River basins. The two members of the H. cochliodon group differ from one another in color (gray with widely spaced black spots vs. dark brown with more numerous spots) and tooth morphology (large spoon-shaped teeth vs. small spoon-shaped teeth). The new Hypancistrus differs from H. inspector by having smaller, more numerous spots. The new members of the H. cochliodon group and the new Hypancistrus appear to be restricted to the Essequibo and/or Negro systems. The new Peckoltia differs substantially in morphology from all other species of Peckoltia and the closely related Hemiancistrus (elongate vs. stout), and it lacks any characteristics to place it in any of the described genera of the Hypostominae. The species is known from the Essequibo, the Takutu, and the Orinoco River basins.

22961: Several studies have demonstrated the existence of niche differentiation and guild structure in taxonomically diverse anuran assemblages. The theory of limiting similarity established the idea that competition prevents coexistence of species that are morphologically too similar. We evaluated ecological variables such as: microhabitat, diet (prey type and sizes), time activity and reproductive phenology of eight species of genus Eleutherodactylus in a cloud forest on the Cordillera Oriental (Colombia). Seven of these species belong to the group unistrigatus. All of these are similar in morphology and body size. The only species of different phylogenetic group is E. douglasi (galdi group). To evaluate whether resource segregation exist in this assemblage, non parametric variance analysis and null models (pseudocommunity analysis) were performed. Both analyses showed high overlaps, and the pseudocommunity analysis revealed that resource utilization was random, indicating no guild structure. The species perch on leaves at heights among 1.5 and 2.00 m of the ground and are nocturnal active. Comparisons of prey to the ordinal level indicated that this assemblage has not dietary specialists. However, a light segregation of the species of different phylogenetic group was observed. E. douglasi was collected and listened throughout the day and consumed smaller spiders than the others species. Additionally, this species was not collected or listened at the beginning of the dry time, whereas the others appear throughout the year suggesting differentiation in the reproductive time. The overlapping in the use of the evaluated resources in this assemblage with closely related species and with a history of co-occurrence, suggests that the competitive effects are minimal.

22962: Until recently, our knowledge of the Australasian freshwater turtle fauna was poor, and their classification remains in drastic need of review. Lack of knowledge has been a major impediment to conservation and has limited our understanding of how freshwater turtle biodiversity is distributed across the Australasian landscape. The situation has in the last decade with detailed surveys and analysis of species boundaries using allozyme electrophoresis and the subsequent formal description of a number of new species. Robust phylogenies for the fauna have been established using a combination of allozyme electrophoresis and mitochondrial and nuclear gene sequences. Highlights of recent research include (a) that the Australasian and South American chelid radiations are probably independent (reciprocally monophyletic); (b) a doubling of the number of recognised species; (c) identification of sibling species (formerly cryptic); (d) evidence of natural hybridisation across even disparate taxa; (e) patterns of distribution of species that reflects historical patterns of sea level change (New Guinea-Australia connection); and (f) substantial divergence of populations within species, with patterns that can be explained by historical patterns of Pleistocene climate change. In this talk I will outline how we addressed the problems of delineating species within the Australasian fauna, how these species are distributed across the Australian continent and adjacent region, where the hotspots are for biodiversity and endemism, and how we have interpreted these patterns in terms of the history of our island continent.
22963: Using a matched pairs study design, we compare abundance and assemblage of lotic amphibians in late-seral and second-growth redwood forests to consider the long-term recovery of amphibian populations following timber harvest. The study was conducted in two separate redwood forests (about 100 miles apart) with three matched pairs of streams per forest. The second-growth forests (treatment, n = 6) are 37-60 years old, and the late-seral forests (control, n = 6) retain 80% or more unharvested trees in the drainage area above the study sites. Relevant environmental factors were measured throughout the sampling period. Nocturnal visual encounter surveys for amphibians occurred in three seasons for two years. Pairing streams and randomizing sampling dates helped control for confounding factors. Results from the first year of data suggest that amphibian diversity and abundance was greater in streams draining late-seral forests, while streams draining second-growth forests had greater fine sediment loads. Adding a second year of data offers further support for the argument and allows for comparison between years.

22964: Ambystoma talpoideum, commonly known as the mole salamander, reaches the northern extremities of its range in western Kentucky. As a facultatively paedomorphic species, A. talpoideum presents an opportunity to study the comparative life histories and potential interactions of metamorphic and paedomorphic individuals within the same population. The focus of this research was to locate potential breeding sites of A. talpoideum in western Kentucky and to observe breeding patterns within these populations. Paedomorphic individuals have been confirmed at two sites in rural Calloway County and at one of twelve potential sites in Land Between the Lakes (LBL). Breeding activity (indicated by cloacal swelling and the presence of spermatophores) at the LBL site concluded by mid-February 2002. No metamorphic salamanders were found at this site until December 2002. Metamorphic individuals were discovered at the Calloway County sites in December 2001 and 2002, and have shown signs of breeding activity during the same time frame as paedomorphic individuals. Breeding at the Calloway County sites continued through February 2002 and waned in early March 2002 during the first year of study. The timing of breeding is atypical because previous studies have shown that paedomorphic individuals generally begin and cease breeding earlier than metamorphic individuals. Exceptions have been noted when paedomorphic salamanders have only recently reached maturity. Current analysis of paedomorphic versus metamorphic snout-vent length (SVL) measurements supports this hypothesis and suggests that paedomorphosis may be a temporary strategy for mole salamanders in these ponds.

22965: Phenotypic plasticity is an environment-specific expression of an organism's genotype. In amphibians, there has been a growing interest in the plasticity of external morphology in response to predators and competitors and how these changes affect amphibian performance. However, there has been little attention paid to how predators and competitors simultaneously affect the internal morphology of amphibians. If critical shifts in organ morphology occur in different environments, then this could be an important, yet neglected area of plasticity. We examined the relative gut length of wood frog tadpoles (Rana sylvatica) in the presence of intra- and interspecific competition (Pseudacris triseriata). Intra- and interspecific competitors both reduced wood frog growth, although intraspecific competition had a larger negative effect. At the same time, wood frogs facing higher competition developed relatively longer intestines. This phenotypic change appears to be an adaptive response because it results in increased wood frog growth. The ability to alter relative intestine length could be the underlying mechanism that tadpoles use to improve their fitness and may alter competitive outcomes in aquatic communities. This more integrated view of morphological plasticity is shedding new light on the way we conceptualize amphibian plasticity and the underlying mechanisms of competition.

22966: Sixty-six species of lizards and amphisbaenians (Reptilia: Squamata) are known from the state of Pará, in northern Brazil, of which 40 occur mainly in Amazonia and six are known only from relatively restricted areas in the state. Two species deserve special attention – Stenocercus dumerilii is endemic to Amazonia eastern of Tocantins River, while Gonatodes eladioi seems to be restricted to Serra dos Carajás, both areas under high human pressure. As an example, only 2% of the original Amazonian forest is left in the Bragantine Region east of Belém, an area with 11000 Km2 (Nepstad, et al., 1996, in J. Schelhas & R. Greenberg (eds.), Forest patches in tropical landscapes, Washington DC, Island Press); a mosaic of woody second growth, agricultural clearings and pasture now covers the remaining area. The varzea (Amazonian floodplains) along the Amazon, which harbors a special fauna, is another environment extensively modified for cattle ranching. Moreover, even forested areas are subjected to increasing logging pressure, and the effects of these changes on the fauna are not yet completely understood. The evaluation of the conservation status of the lizard fauna in the state of Pará is based on the known distribution of these animals and on the degree of conservation of the different vegetation types where they occur. IUCN red list categories are used, taking into consideration peculiarities due to the regional scale of the analysis. This study is part of the Amazonian Biodiversity Program of Museu Paraense Emilio Goeldi and the associated project Biota Pará, made in collaboration with Conservation International do Brasil.

22967: Lizards of the genus Teius are distributed in southern South America along a wide variety of habitats, from the dry desert Monte in western Argentina to the humid plains near Selva Paranaense in the Parana Basin. Currently only three species have been described, T. teyou in the western Chaco and Monte, T. oculatus in the eastern Pampas and Espinal, and the parthenogenetic T. suquiensis distributed in the central range of both species. Several individuals of the three species from several localities were included in a molecular phylogenetic analysis of the origin of the parthenogenetic populations. Two nuclear (C-MOS, Enolase intron), and one mitochondrial (ND4) genes were used as markers, for a total of approximately 1500 bp. Fixed differences were identified for the sexual species in both nuclear genes, and these were always present as polymorphisms in T. suquiensis, suggesting the hybrid origin of this species. Sequences for the mitochondrial fragment always were identical to those from T. oculatus, indicating that a female T. oculatus and a male of T. teyou were the parental ancestors.

22968: Despite snakes are very important not only concerning conservationism, but also because this group comprises poisonous animals involved with human health, the knowledge about snake natural history is scarce for some regions of Brazil such as the Pantanal. Among the poisonous snakes, the neurotoxins of true coral snakes (most species included in the genus Micrurus) deserve distinction. In Pantanal M. pyrrhocryptus (family Elapidae) is little known and there are several different opinions about its taxonomic status. The natural history of M. pyrrhocryptus was studied from August 2001 to July 2002 in different altitudes in a semi-decidual forest of Santa Cruz hill, Macico do Urucum, Corumba, MS, by means of collects and pitfalls. We also used specimens deposited in scientific collections from other locations. Only the specimens captured in Macico do Urucum were used in analyses of reproduction, diet and parasitism. Fourteen specimens were analyzed, being nine from Santa Cruz hill, one from Corumba and four from Argentina. The specimens from Corumba identified as M. pyrrhocryptus extended the geographic distribution of the species. Food items were not found in the stomachs of the snakes, which presented a 60 per cent prevalence of parasites in the stomach and intestines. Females were even more (75 per cent) infested by nematodes in their stomach and intestines, besides other two types of parasites (10 per cent of nematodes in the lungs and 10 per cent of platelmintes in the mouth). The species presents sexual dimorphism regarding the tail length and number of subcaudals, both larger in males. According to evidences recorded here, although this is a preliminary study, the reproductive cycle is annual and recruitment happens during the summer.

22969: The decline of several amphibian populations all over the world due to their high sensibility to alterations of habitat and their skin semi-permeability causes us to worry about the conservation of their biodiversity. Besides, there is the risk of losing peculiar substances present in the skin of the amphibians, which have a great pharmacological potential, and the environmental imbalance provoked by the alteration of the food chains. The urban growing is one of the main causes indicated for that decline because it leads to contamination, elimination and fragmentation of habitats. The disordered development allied to the lack of knowledge about amphibians, mainly anurans, may irreversibly damage this fauna. The utilization of vocalization of animals (birds, amphibians, mammals) may offer great contributions to the knowledge of the fauna, being a fast way to carry out environmental evaluations. The richness and intensity of vocalization of anurans in urban areas of Corumba was studied from February 2002 to January 2003 in a secondary forest and surroundings of a temporary lagoon. We used a transect with four stop sites on which the presence of species and the intensity of vocalization were recorded according to NAAMP index. The turn when vocalization happened was also recorded. We recorded 16 species of four families: Bufonidae (2), Hylidae (7), Microhylidae (1) and Leptodactylidae (6). The reproduction of these species was correlated to the rainy season, from December to March (r2 = 0.80). The species that presented greater intensity of vocalization were Scinax aff. ruber and Physalaemus albonotatus, with peaks during January. The species that presented the greater period of vocalization was Leptodactylus fuscus, from September to February. The species concentrate the activity of calls from 7:00 p.m to 11:00 p.m.

22970: The draughtboard shark Cephaloscyllium laticeps is the most common catshark in the coastal waters off Southern Australia where it is a major higher trophic level predator of temperate reef ecosystems. It is caught as bycatch in lobster traps, demersal trawls, long-line and gillnets. There is currently no targeted commercial fishery for draughtboard sharks, although recently a small number of commercial gill net fishers are trialing the species on the local market. Because draughtboard sharks have a high catchability in traps and gillnets they are potentially vulnerable to population reduction through fishing. Assessing the potential impact of fishing mortality is currently hindered by the lack of knowledge of draughtboard shark biology. The purpose of this study is to investigate specific aspects of life history and biology of draughtboard sharks that will help future management decisions. In addition to collecting reproductive data from dead specimens, hormonal levels have been analysed from blood samples as a means of describing reproductive condition in live animals. Plasma levels of progesterone, testosterone (T) and 17- βestradiol in females, and T in males were obtained measured by RIA. Stomach content analysis is being used to quantify prey items and biases associated with different fishing gears (gillnets and traps). Preliminary attempts to age the sharks using vertebral ring counts have been problematic. Local movement patterns are being investigated using traditional fin tags and acoustic tags. The fin tags have confirmed that proportions of sharks are recaptured in the same area each year. The acoustic tagged sharks are being caught, tagged and released within an array of acoustic receivers that will enable us to follow their daily movements on and adjacent to the reef system.
22971: The occurrence of twinning in turtles has been known for many years and relatively well documented for some species. This fact is already published to Trachemys dorbignyi, besides the two known occurrences have happened to incubation eggs in artificial conditions. Thus, it will be presented information about the first two-headed hatchling occurrence of a Trachemys dorbignyi collected in the nature. The individual was found in Pelotas city, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. There is not much detailed information about the environment where the specimen was found due to the fact the animal has been collected by laymen. The animal was active being able to feed itself independently through both heads. The hatchling kept alive during four months and died for drowning. The joint between the turtles happened along all the lateral of carapace extension and in a part of plastron. The animal structure presented a tail, two posterior limbs, three anterior limbs, two heads, a single plastron and two pseudo-carapaces. The third anterior limb, located between the two heads presented the structure of two limbs. There was only an insertion point of the yolk sac in the plastron. The only anomaly in the number of scutes in the plastron was the presence of four gular scutes. The number of scutes in the carapace was significantly bigger than the usual pattern of the specie. Each pseudo-carapace presented all the vertebral scutes, even if dislocated, a set of costal scutes and half of the marginal scutes. The other scutes were fused forming a central crest. The internal morphology analysis was not made to evaluate the organs compositions.

22972: A literature survey was conducted to determine the Amphibian diversity and distribution in Brazilian Amazonia. Patterns of endemisms and similarity of fauna between localities were also addressed. Twenty-eight inventories were found for the region, the majority localized in areas with easier access by road or river. A minimum of 163 amphibian species was recorded for Brazilian Amazonia. The results indicated that many species are endemic to the Amazonian lowlands as an entity, but the patterns of species uniqueness among sites suggested low endemic distribution within the lowlands of the Amazon Basin. The mean similarity between localities varied from low to intermediate (mean = 0.40), indicating that the Brazilian Amazonia is characterized by distinctive assemblages of amphibians throughout its extension. Localities further apart had lower similarity. No threatened species were recorded. We suggest that areas next to the Amazon deforestation frontier should be prioritized for new studies due to the high rate of alteration and potential loss of species. Additionally, there are few studies on Amphibian population dynamics in Brazilian Amazonia and more of them should be emphasize to help to draw a better picture of the status of Amphibians in this region.

22973: Some species of anuran amphibians, such as the Brazilian toad Bufo ictericus, possess a calcified dermal layer (the as Ebert-Katschenko layer) located between the stratum spongiosum and the stratum compactum. It has been regarded as a protective barrier against desiccation or involved in storage and mobilization of calcium or as a barrier for the interchange of substances between the animal’s internal and external environment. The Bufo ictericus integument was removed from ventral and dorsal region and examined through light microscopy and analytical electron microscopy. The intermediary layer is strongly basophilic through HE technique, exhibiting a metachromatic reaction after the DMB technique. In association with previous biochemical results realized in the Bufo ictericus skin, where hyaluronic acid and dermatan sulfate (glycosaminoglycans) were detected, it is possible to conclude that the metachromatic reaction correspond to dermatan sulfate. Through the Van Kossa method the presence of calcium was also revealed in this intermediary basophilic layer. Correlating these observations we conclude that the calcium deposits and the glycosaminoglycans coexist in the same place, namely the Ebert- Katschenko layer.

22974: This work describes the reproductive cycle of Diapoma terofali (Eigenmann 1915), an inseminating characid species of the tribe Diapomini of the Glandulocaudinae. The reproductive period is estimated through the analysis of the monthly variation of the mean of the gonadosomatic index (GSI) and of the relative frequencies of gonadal maturation stages. The correlations between GSI means variation and day-length, water temperature and rainfall are tested. The relative and total fecundity are described. A total of 217 males and 247 females, collected monthly between April 2001 and January 2002 in the Rio Ibicui da Faxina, Rio Uruguay drainage, RS, Brazil, have been analyzed. Preliminary results demonstrate that the GSI means of males increases in September while female GSI means increases in October. This is coincident with the higher observed frequencies of mature or late maturation specimens. Spearman test demonstrates a statistically significant correlation only between GSI means and day-length for both sexes. The reproductive period of Diapoma terofali is seasonal, corresponding to spring and summer in the Southern hemisphere, similar to that observed in most characid species, including other glandulocaudines. Day-length seems to be the trigger factor to maturation, but it is possibly influenced also by temperature increase

22975: When compared with ectothermic shark species, lamnid sharks have higher activities of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) in the fast, glycolytic myotomal muscle (white muscle, WM) used to power high-speed bursts. Lamnid sharks produce large amounts of lactate from WM glycogen, which may subsequently be oxidized or used to resynthesize glycogen. In fishes, it is believed that gluconeogenesis occurs within the WM, yet the gluconeogenic potential of lamnid shark tissues has not been reported. To assess this, we measured the activity of four enzymes required for gluconeogenesis (pyruvate carboxylase, malic enzyme, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase, and fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase) in the WM, liver, red muscle (slow, oxidative muscle), and heart ventricle of the short-fin mako shark (Isurus oxyrinchus). Pyruvate carboxylase was not detected in any tissue samples. Malic enzyme activity was highest in the heart and red muscle of the mako shark. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate activity was greatest in the liver and white muscle tissues. Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase activity was greatest in the liver tissue and was not detected in WM. Because pyruvate carboxylase was not detected, it appears that none of the four tissues studied can carry out gluconeogenesis using the pathway known to occur in other vertebrates. However, if the reaction catalyzed by pyruvate kinase (PK) can be reversed, as has been suggested for teleosts, then gluconeogenesis may be possible. Because the PK activity is high in mako shark WM, we are currently investigating if the WM PK can catalyze the conversion of pyruvate to phosphoenolpyruvate for gluconeogenesis.

22976: The critically endangered southern California mountain yellow-legged frog (Rana muscosa) continues to decline in well-protected areas in southern California. Historically, this frog occurred across 4 mountains ranges and in over 40 creeks. Currently, they occur in seven streams across 3 mountain ranges. We have estimated the adult population size at all seven remain locations which range from the smallest population at 6 adults to the largest population with 52 adults, 3 of these location have less than 15 estimated adults. Lack of information on this frogs natural history has lead to disagreements among regional agencies on how best to conserve this species. From the summer of 2000 through present, USGS has conducted extensive surveys across the Angeles and San Bernardino National Forests, California, that has greatly increased our understanding of this species; including habitat requirements, phenology, potential threats, movement patterns, current size and distribution. Currently, population expansion is unlikely for several reasons. Our repeated field observation suggest that, the two greatest pressures restricting dispersal and limiting population survival include 1) lack of perennial water, due to several consecutive drought years, and 2) where water is available, the presence of exotic trout. Our data show that frogs do not travel far from water and exhibit high site fidelity. With this new information we are able to help refine an ongoing conservation strategy for the southern California mountain yellow-legged frog.

22977: It was analyzed data from 33 nests of Hydromedusa tectifera collected from 1999 to 2002 in different geographic areas in the extreme South of Brazil. The data were related to the females and to the nest environment aiming to present the first survey about the reproductive ecology of the specie. The specie has a timing of nesting of, approximately, 50 days, with its beginning in the first days of November and ending in the second half of December. The mean of eggs in each nest is 11 (Min.=2; Max. = 21; S.D.= 4.01; n=24), having the modal class the same value. The eggs are white, hard, elliptics and have a sphericity of 0.66. It has an mean of 36.5mm in length (Min.=31mm; Max.=43mm; S.D.=1.91; n= 269), 24mm in width (Min.=20.7mm; Max.=26.1mm; S.D.=1.00; n=270) and 12.5g in weight (Min.= 8.8g; Max.=16g; S.D.=1.29; n=170). Linear regressions showed that the weight of the eggs are more related to its width (r2=0.62) than to the length (r2=0.50). The nests are laid, approximately, 9.9m from the water shore (Min.=0.7m; Max.=63.1m; S.D.=11.01; n=33). Approximately 36% of the nests are laid in less of 5m from the water and 88% of the nestings happen in distances shorter than 15m from the shore. The specie use to lay the clutch in high incline areas and on the base of vegetation formed by bushes. It was observed that the nests are established in areas that present an average incline of 26.7° (Min.=0; Max.=55; S.D.=12.5; n=33). Most of the nests (52%) are located in areas that have an incline between 20° and 35°. The nesting time starts at 5:00 p.m. until approximately 10:00 p.m., however 54% of the captures happened between 7:00 p.m., and 21:00 p.m. The road-kill females indicated that the specie could make more than one clutch in each reproductive season, nevertheless this conclusion was not proved in the nature yet.

22978: It was analyzed 111 individuals of Hydromedusa tectifera captured in four different areas in the extreme South of Rio Grande do Sul State. 22979: The knowledge of the biology and reproductive ecology of a species is fundamental to the development of methods of management and conservation. Based on this fact it was realized seven years of collects (1995-2001) monitorings in the Taim Ecological Station, a Federal protected area, aiming to study the reproductive ecology of Trachemys dorbignyi. It was verified that the specie presents a reproductive period that begins in October and lasts until the beginning of January. October and November are considered the most intense period of nesting. The number of eggs in each nest can vary from 6 to 19 eggs, having a mean of 12.1 ± 2.4 (n=93). The length mean of the eggs was 39.3mm ± 2.06 and the width was 25.8mm ± 1.07 and the weight was 14.9g ± 1.47. The number of eggs is positively related to the maximum length of the carapace (F1,41=11.850 p < 0.001), nevertheless the correlation between both variables is relatively low (r2=0.474) probably this low correlation happens due to the number of eggs are more related to the body mass of the female and the environmental variations. During each reproductive period until three layings can be done, divided into an interval of 15 days among each one. The only information available about the variation of clutch size during the consecutive laying showed 12 eggs laid in the first clutch, and 14 in the second, which happened a month later. It was calculated the percentile of females of the population that nesting each year and it was concluded that only 31% of the females have reproductive activity in each reproductive period. This value is probably sub-estimated due to some sample problems, however it demonstrates that the specie has a reproductive cycle each two years.

22980: It was analyzed the capacity of movement, direction and fidelity to the nest site of a population of Trachemys dorbignyi in the South of Brazil. 22981: The characterization of a population of Trachemys dorbignyi in natural environment was done focusing on the sexual aspects, structure of the population, morphology and sexual dimorphisms. The study area was located in the town of Rio Grande, on the coastal plain of the State of Rio Grande do Sul – Brazil. The area is formed by a great number of coastal lakes associated to wetlands and fields. The results presented a sexual rate of 1.02 males for each female and a prevalence of females as regards their body mass. The males are approximately 14% smaller than the females when the medium values of the length of the carapaces are compared (mean LC male=181.6mm; mean LC female=212.1mm) (F1,207 = 191.140; p < 0.001). The specie presents evident secondary sexual dimorphisms, the males have melanism and their tail is longer than the females that have the same size they do. The only measure in which the male presented a better average than the female is the VÃO (distance between the posterior portion of the midventral suture of the anal scutes and the posterior portion of the suture of the supratails scutes), was considered an excellent variable to the sexual difference in inferior sizes related to other measures or morphological characteristics. A discriminant analysis, which used 6 morphometric variables and 66 turtles (44 males and 22 females) defined a classification matrix that presented 100% of rights sexes for both, and also showed an explaining degree of 89% and a significance of p < 0.001 (Wilk's lambda = 0.205; χ2 = 96.567; d.f. = 6). This analyze identified the VÃO, and the width of the anterior lobe, as the most important variable in the characterization of the males, the head width and the height of the carapace as the female determiners. The sexual maturity was estimated from the difference between the linear regressions built for gender. It was verified it occurs approximately when it has reached a length of 130 mm in the carapaces of male and between 150 and 160 mm in the females.
