22982: The Brazilian legislation establishes different areas of protection to the vegetal formation associated to the shore of aquatic environments. The widths of these areas depend on the width of the aquatic environment and its genesis. It was compared the values established by the legislations with the known distances of the nests and nesting females. The positions were obtained with a gps and the distance of the water was calculated inserting the points through a digital map of the study area. It was also analyzed which protected area was required to protect 90% of nests of each species. Data from 173 nests and 841 Trachemys dorbignyi females, 34 nests and 73 Phrynops hilarii females, 30 nests and 20 Hydromedusa tectifera females were used in this survey. The nests and T. dorbignyi females are located in a mean of 63.5 m from the water (Min.= 0 m; Max.= 607 m; n = 1014). P. hilarii presented a mean of 58.6 m (Min.= 1.2 m; Max.= 316.3 m; n = 107) and H. tectifera 16.0 m (Min.= 0.2 m; Max.= 92.3 m; n=51). It was verified that T. dorbignyi is the specie that most width requires to achieve the score of 90% of protection, 140m of the shore. P. hilarii requires 110 m and H. tectifera needs only 30 m. T. dorbignyi is the most abundant specie and occupies a bigger number of habitats in the study area and is considered the most demanding specie, as regards the width of the nest sites. The results showed that the Brazilian legislation only succeeds effectively in the protection of the nest sites located in rivers that measure from 200 to 600 m width. It is considered inefficient to the turtles due to the reduced number of environments that present this characteristic in the area of geographic distribution.

22983: The collects were done in three different areas in the South of the State of Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. The turtles were captured manually while walking in the area. 22984: World-wide concern for amphibian populations has focused research on documenting amphibian distributions and habitat associations over large geographic areas. Most programs involve sampling potential habitats using a wide variety of techniques to document species occurrence and relative abundance. Population declines may be inferred by a decrease in the number of sites win which a species is detected. These methods assume constant (often perfect) species detectability over time, space, and among different sampling methods. We utilized recent developments in capture-recapture theory to estimate proportion of sites occupied and species detection probabilities for a suite of salamanders found in Great Smoky Mountains National Park. We included large-scale habitat characteristics (e.g., elevation, vegetation type, and stream presence) as site and sampling covariates. We explored differences among area-constrained and coverboard sampling techniques. We found species-specific differences in detection probability ranging from 0.26-0.72. Detection probabilities were lower for coverboards than area-constrained searches for all terrestrial species. Habitat characteristics were important in both site occupancy and detection probabilities but varied among species. Nevertheless, the identification of important habitat characteristics was consistent among sampling methods. We strongly recommend incorporating detectability estimation into research studies designed to document presence and spatial distribution of amphibian species.

22985: The antipredator behaviors of Phaeognathus hubrichti (Red Hills salamander), a large fossorial plethodontid, and the basal member of the Desmognathine salamanders, are unknown. When contacted by a snake tongue-flick, P. hubrichti exhibits several antipredator behaviors including immobility, gape, walk, run, head flatten, head elevate, flip, bite, writhe, and flinch. The antipredator behaviors of Phaeognathus are more similar to those species in its sister taxon (Desmognathus), than to those of other less closely related fossorial salamanders. Gape, a threat display, is nearly identical to that of Desmognathus quadramaculatus. Gape, bite, and writhe are proposed to be ancestral behaviors in this group.

22986: One of the most rare habitats in the Gulf of California is made up of hard coral. These patches or isolated coral heads (mainly of the Pocillopora genus) have a distinct abundance at different spatial scales. The coral hawkfish Cirrhitichthys oxycephalus is not an obligate symbiotic species on coral heads, but it is the dominant in terms of abundance and biomass. We assume that the spatial distribution and the size of coral heads determine the dynamic population of the species. The abundance of coral heads at a scale of thousands of meters (site scale) is more important than the differences among regions at a scale of tens of kilometers for explaining hawkfish distribution. There is a negative exponential relationship between density of hawkfish with density of coral heads. The trend of juveniles/adults rate was to increase with the size of coral heads. However, the records of the greatest juveniles/adults rates occurred among the sites with the higher coverage of coral. The temporal pattern of the density of C. oxycephalus showed no differences among sites, and the small juveniles were present in all the sampling seasons. In a scenario of low density of coral heads one head represents precious shelter, increasing the interactions among hawkfish individuals and with other species.

22987: Specimens of the Bufo crucifer species group deposited in 13 collections were analyzed morphologically. The analysis of the external morphologic characters of the different populations demonstrated the existence of five valid species with different geographical distributions. The statistical analysis of the morphometric characters confirmed these species satisfactorily. The list of synonyms for the available names was well resolved, and two new species were described. This group of the genus Bufo, previously considered as composed only by B. crucifer, now includes the following species: Bufo crucifer, Bufo ornatus, Bufo henseli, Bufo abei sp. nov. and Bufo pombali sp. nov.. Bufo crucifer is distributed in areas of the Atlantic Forest in the states of the Northeastern region of Brasil and the State of Espírito Santo, B. ornatus in the states of Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo, B. henseli in the plateau of the states of Rio Grande do Sul and Santa Catarina, B. abei sp. nov. along the coast of the states of Paraná and Santa Catarina, and B. pombali sp. nov. in the State of Minas Gerais.

22988: The inventories of snake diversity in Brazil have been considered insufficient and scarce. There are not even punctual studies about the herpetofaunistic composition of the Southern Grasslands. The region of Serra do Sudeste, southern Brazil, is characterized by the presence of steppes in an environment that presents seasonal climate, shallow and sandy soil, generally plane relief and vegetation with shrubby savanna and gallery forests. We describe in this study the snakes richness and abundance from detached areas (1500 hectares) with open formations and gallery forests, which are altered by agriculture and cattle raising activities, in Dom Feliciano and Encruzilhada do Sul Municipalities. We found 471 snakes of 27 species from January 2000 to December 2002 using three methods to collect: pitfalls (PFT), visual search limited by time (TCS) and resident collector (RC). During 720 days and nights while the pitfalls were open, 106 snakes of 20 species were captured. PFT: during 1292 hours-man of search 109 snakes of 20 species were captured. RC: during 24 months 275 snakes of 21 species were captured. Although still preliminary, this study shows that the RC method presents greater efficiency if the richness and abundance of the biological material sampled is considered, being followed by TCS and PFT. The three methods were complementary to each other regarding richness, however, the abundance was three times greater with RC method. It is important to remember the objectives and methods used in these cases, once sometimes the result of a given method is not valid for a given objective. For example, studies about diet using individuals captured using pitfalls are controversial. Compared to other similar studies under development in southern Brazil, this study has found the greater species richness until this moment.

22989: The Neotropical genus Atractus comprises approximately 80 species widely distributed in South America. Atractus reticulatus is a fossorial, small snake (maximum total length = 390 mm in females, 279 mm in males) that occurs in Paraguay, northeastern Argentina, and southern Brazil. Similarly to most species of Atractus, the available data on the natural history of A. reticulatus come from opportunistic observations. We analyzed the gonads of 42 females, 43 males and 10 unsexed hatchlings from the eastern Central Depression of the State of Rio Grande do Sul. Clutches of three captive individuals were also included in the analysis. The sexual maturity and reproductive cycle of females were based on the diameter of the largest vitellogenic follicles (6 mm or more = mature) and their seasonal distribution, and oviposition. Fecundity was estimated by counting vitellogenic follicles and eggs. Males were considered mature when the deferent ducts were convoluted. The smallest mature female had 242 mm of snout-vent length (SVL), and the smallest male, 198 mm. The reproduction is seasonal, with vitellogenesis occurring from August to December. Clutches were observed from December to January, and recruitment from January to March. One female dissected just after laying eggs had vitellogenic follicles, indicating the possibility of occurrence of multiple clutches. The mean number of vitellogenic follicles (n = 8) and eggs (n = 3) was 3.6. The fecundity of A. reticulatus is low if compared to colubrids in general. However, their eggs are proportionally large (mean length = 31.2 mm, mean weight = 1.44 g, n = 7), and their clutches are heavy, corresponding to approximately 46.7 % of the female weight. Three hatchlings were born after 66 days of artificial incubation; their mean SVL was 116.3 mm and their mean weight was 1.31 g.

22990: Turtle species in South Dakota have received little attention since the 1960's. Beginning in 1985, much of South Dakota has been subjected to higher than average water conditions that would enable greater travel and survival conditions for turtles. To test this hypothesis, we began a 2-year statewide survey project on the distribution of turtles within the state. Seven possible turtle species include: the false map (Graptemys pseudogeographica), smooth softshell (Apalone mutica), spiny softshell (Apalone spinifera), western painted (Chrysemys picta bellii), snapping (Chelydra serpentina), ornate box (Terrapene ornata), and Blanding's turtle (Emydoidea blandingii). The ornate box turtle only occurs in western South Dakota. In May-August 2002, turtles were collected in streams, lakes, rivers, and wetlands in 44 counties east of the Missouri River. Basking traps, baited hoop nets, crab traps, and hand capture techniques were used to capture turtles. Hoop nets baited with fresh fish were the most effective method. We sampled 250 sites and captured 476 turtles representing 5 species: 7 false map turtles were captured in lake and riverine habitats, 11 smooth and 24 spiny softshells were captured in riverine habitats only, and 361 western painted turtles and 73 snapping turtles were captured in a variety of stream, lake, riverine, and wetland habitats. Blanding's turtles may occur in extreme eastern South Dakota, but none were captured or seen by us in 2002. Species distribution for western painted, snapping, and false map turtles were very similar to those reported in the 1960's; however, our data extended the distributional range for the spiny softshell by 322 km (200 miles). In contrast, our data indicated that the distributional range of the smooth softshell had decreased by about 193 km (120 miles). During May-August 2003, turtle surveys will be conducted in the 22 counties west of the Missouri River.

22991: The aim of this study was to analyze the reproduction of Apareiodon affinis in the Rio Ibicuí, located between Cacequi and São Vicente, RS, Brazil. The specimens (131 females and 114 males) were collected monthly, from April/2001 to March/2002. The fishes were collected with a seine net, preserved in 10% formalin in the field and transferred to 70% ethanol in laboratory. The reproductive period was determined through the analysis of the monthly variation of the mean of the Gonadosomatic Index (GSI). Fecundity was estimated through oocytes count in 13 mature gonads. 22992: We analyzed fish abundance and environmental data collected over nine years from six side channels of the unimpounded upper Mississippi River (UMR) between river km 46.7 and 128.7. A partial canonical correspondence analysis revealed differences in fish assemblages and environmental factors correlated with the six side channels. Fishes correlated with open side channels represented large river species tolerant of current and/or turbidity. 22993: We report on a new lantern shark belonging to a group of larger Etmopterus species that includes the nominal species E. baxteri, E. granulosus, and E. princeps. 22994: Previous attempts to resolve phylogenetic relationships of ictiobines based on molecular sequence data, suggest that congeneric species are hybridizing where sympatric in the Mississippi River Basin. 22995: In 1944 Myers described two spineless glanapterygine trichomycterid catfishes, Pygidianops eigenmanni and Typhlobelus ternetzi, from sand in the Sao Gabriel rapids during the dry season in the upper Rio Negro, Brasil. We discovered four additional undescribed species, two in each of the above genera. Two species, one of each genus, co-occur in the Orinoco Delta region in bottom trawls via a plankton net that inadvertently hit the bottom. Almost all of these net hauls also contained sand and gravel. Two additional species, one of each genus, were recently discovered in the Rio Cuao, upper Orinoco River. All specimens of these latter two species were found within clean sand, which they may never leave, during the end of the dry season of an exceptionally dry year. They were captured by hand, scooping sand using a small mesh dip net and picking through the sand to find the fishes, whose life color matched the sand. Two additional undescribed glanapterygines have also been found in the Amazon basin from similar habitat. In both Orinoco sites, both species co-occur in the same net samples. An additional tiny trichomycterid, Sarcoglanis simplex, also originally discovered from the Sao Gabriel rapids, was also found in the sand with the Cuao glanapterygines. These fishes may be part of the meiofauna community, although too large to be considered true meiofauna. Morphological features consistent with this habitat are present in these species. We speculate that they may be widely and perhaps continuously distributed in the bottom sands of at least the Amazon-Orinoco system, as partly suggested by Costa and Brockman, and may be very common in this difficult to sample habitat. They could form a trophic link between the true meiofauna and higher trophic levels via electric fishes such as Gymnorhamphichthys, also found in the sand with the Cuao glanapterygines.

22996: The dourada (Brachyplatystoma flavicans) is among the two most important catfish species in the Amazon, being captured by both artesanal and commercial fishing fleets from Iquitos (Peru) to the estuary of the Amazonas river, in Belem. Studies by several authors suggest that the species has differentiated areas for feeding/growth and reproduction, and that, in the Amazon, it is composed by a single population that seasonally migrates from the feeding and growing areas to the areas of reproduction. The main objectives of this study were: to estimate the genetic variability among and between individuals of B. flavicans collected in three points along the Estuary-Amazonas-Solimoes axis (EAS) and to verify if the variability found was correlated with geographic distribution. A fragment of 1037 bp corresponding to the D-loop of the mtDNA was sequenced for 15 individuals in three locations: Belem, Manaus and Leticia. The sequences were utilized in four types of analyses: phylogenetic (parsimony, maximum likelihood and distance), DNA polymorphism, AMOVA and Nested Clade Analyses. It was possible to identify 31 haplotypes and 27 singletons among the 45 B. flavicans individuals sequenced. The larger genetic variability was found in Belem and the smaller in Leticia, but there was no correlation between the genetic variability and geographic distribution, suggesting that B. flavicans enclose a single migrating population in the EAS axis. However, as an explanation for the significantly larger degree of genetic variability found in Belem, one cannot discard the hypothesis that different subpopulations of B. flavicans may segregate geographically and genetically in the basins of the different afluents of the EAS system, during the migration for reproduction.

22997: I studied some parameters of the reproductive ecology and factors that influence egg survivorship of Podocnemis erythrocephala (Spix, 1824) in four "campina" habitats at the mouth of Aiuana River, Tapuruquara Environmental Protection Area, Santa Isabel do Rio Negro municipality, Amazonas State, Brazil (S 00° 31' 55.6", W 64° 55' 11.5"). The lizard preyed on nests less than 10 days old, that were up to 10m away from the "campina" border.

22998: Data collection in scientific research studies can be a labor-intensive process. Many researchers spend large quantities of their time simply collecting the specimens they need to conduct a study. It is possible to collect large numbers of samples in a relatively short time while providing meaningful educational opportunities for middle and high school students. This study describes three ichthyologic research projects conducted by University of Hawaii graduate students participating with the NSF-funded Ecology, Evolution, and Conservation Biology Graduate Teaching Fellowship program that employed the assistance of pre-college students. In two of the studies, students primarily assisted in collecting samples for use in the study. In a third, students collected behavioral data. We will discuss both positive and negative aspects of using students to help collect samples or data, and offer suggestions for those wishing to try this exciting technique themselves.

22999: The high diversity of freshwater fish found in the Neotropics is paralleled by a remarkable diversity in body shapes. Morphological diversity indicates adaptations to a large variety of habitats and to biological interactions with other fishes leading to niche diversification. The high diversity of fish morphologies, habitats, and food resources found in tropical areas represent an attractive system for testing ecomorphological hypotheses. In this work I investigated whether or not ecomorphological attributes correlated with fish diets and habitat utilization, to what extent ecomorphology can predict functional feeding groups and the vertical distribution of fish, and whether or not ecomorphological aspects are related to taxonomy. The first two questions were examined using multivariate discriminant and correlation analyses, whereas the third was approached using statistical randomization techniques. The study area was located in central- southeastern Brazil, encompassing two ichthyofaunistic provinces, namely the Upper Parana and High Paraguay. Results revealed that arrays of fish morphological measurements were closely correlated with categories of fish diet and habitat utilization. The ecomorphological approach was able to predict both vertical habitat and diet functional groups of these freshwater fish assemblages. Results also showed that significant correlations between ecomorphological and taxonomic distances were only observed when matrices with a large number of ecomorphological variables were used in the analysis. The success of the ecomorphological approach, i.e., when taxonomic aspects do not interfere in ecological responses, depends on the number and choice of variables used in analyses.
